What is the remainder when P(x) = 4x³ − x + 2 is divided by (2x + 1)?
Show that (x − 2) is a factor of P(x) = x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 and hence factorise P(x) completely. (3 marks)
The polynomial P(x) = x³ + ax² + bx − 6 has (x − 1) as a factor and leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by (x + 1). Find a and b. (3 marks)
Divide P(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x + 1 by (x − 2), and write P(x) in the form (x − 2)Q(x) + R. (3 marks)
Q(x) = x² + 4x + 3 [1]; remainder R = P(2) = 8 + 8 − 10 + 1 = 7 [1]. P(x) = (x − 2)(x² + 4x + 3) + 7 [1]. Check: (x − 2)(x² + 4x + 3) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6, and adding 7 gives P(x).
What is the remainder when P(x) = x³ + 3x² − x + 4 is divided by (x + 2)?
Remainder = P(−2) = −8 + 12 + 2 + 4 = 10. The value 22 is P(2), which would be the remainder for (x − 2).
(x − 3) is a factor of P(x) = x³ − 5x² + kx − 3. What is the value of k?
Need P(3) = 0: 27 − 45 + 3k − 3 = 3k − 21 = 0, so k = 7. Getting −7 comes from a sign slip when collecting terms.
According to the factor theorem, (x − a) is a factor of a polynomial P(x) if and only if
Substituting x = a, the value that makes (x − a) zero, must give P(a) = 0. P(−a) = 0 would instead make (x + a) a factor.
What is the remainder when P(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + x − 7 is divided by (x − 1)?
Remainder = P(1) = 2 − 3 + 1 − 7 = −7. The value −13 is P(−1), which applies to a divisor (x + 1).
Which of the following is a factor of P(x) = x³ + x² − 4x + 2?
P(1) = 1 + 1 − 4 + 2 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor. P(−1), P(2) and P(−2) are all 6, so the other options are not factors.
What is the remainder when P(x) = x⁴ − 3x² + 2x − 1 is divided by (x + 1)?
Remainder = P(−1) = 1 − 3 − 2 − 1 = −5. The value −1 is P(1), the remainder for (x − 1).
What is the remainder when P(x) = 3x³ − 2x² + x + 4 is divided by (3x − 2)?
When P(x) = x³ + kx − 4 is divided by (x + 2) the remainder is −2. What is k?
P(−2) = −8 − 2k − 4 = −2, so −2k = 10 and k = −5. Using P(2) instead would wrongly give k = −3.
When P(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 7 is divided by (x − 3), what is the quotient?
Division gives x² + x − 2 with remainder 1, since (x − 3)(x² + x − 2) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6. The remainder equals P(3) = 1, which is not part of the quotient.
P(x) is a polynomial and P(2) = 0. Which statement must be true?
The remainder when P(x) is divided by (x + 2) is 0
P(2) = 0 means (x − 2) is a factor by the factor theorem. (x + 2) would need P(−2) = 0, which is not given.
(x − 2) is a factor of P(x) = x³ + ax² − x + 6. What is the value of a?
P(2) = 8 + 4a − 2 + 6 = 12 + 4a = 0, so a = −3. A value of 3 comes from losing the negative sign.
What is the remainder when P(x) = 2x³ + 5x² − 4x + 3 is divided by (2x − 1)?
Remainder = P(1/2) = 1/4 + 5/4 − 2 + 3 = 5/2. The value 6 is P(−1/2) and also P(1), which are for different divisors.
What is the remainder when P(x) = x²¹ + 1 is divided by (x + 1)?
Remainder = P(−1) = (−1)²¹ + 1 = −1 + 1 = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor. The value 2 is P(1), the remainder for (x − 1).
Which is the complete factorisation of P(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, given that P(1) = P(2) = P(3) = 0?
Each zero a gives a factor (x − a), so the factors are (x − 1), (x − 2) and (x − 3). Factors of the form (x + a) correspond to zeros at −a, not a.
(x − 1) and (x + 2) are both factors of P(x) = x³ + ax² + bx − 2. What are a and b?
P(1) = 0 gives a + b = 1 and P(−2) = 0 gives 2a − b = 5, so a = 2 and b = −1. The pair a = 3, b = −2 satisfies only the first equation.
A polynomial P(x) of degree 4 is divided by (x − a). The remainder is always
Of the same degree as P(x)
The remainder has smaller degree than the divisor (degree 1), so it is a constant equal to P(a). Degree three describes the quotient, not the remainder.
(x + 1) is a factor of P(x) = 2x³ − x² − 5x + k. What is k?
P(−1) = −2 − 1 + 5 + k = 2 + k = 0, so k = −2. The value 4 comes from using P(1) = k − 4 = 0 instead.
When P(x) is divided by (x − a) the remainder is R. Which of the following must be a factor of P(x) − R?
P(x) − R has value P(a) − R = 0 at x = a, so (x − a) is a factor. R is a value of the polynomial, not a zero.
Find the remainder when P(x) = 2x³ − x² + 3x − 4 is divided by (x + 1). (2 marks)
By the remainder theorem the remainder is P(−1) [1]. P(−1) = −2 − 1 − 3 − 4 = −10 [1].
Show that (x + 3) is a factor of P(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6 and hence factorise P(x) completely. (3 marks)
When P(x) = x³ + kx² − 7x + 6 is divided by (x − 3) the remainder is −6. Find k, and hence find the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x + 1). (3 marks)
Let P(x) = x³ − 3x² − 6x + 8. P(1) = 1 − 3 − 6 + 8 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor [1]. Division gives P(x) = (x − 1)(x² − 2x − 8) [1] = (x − 1)(x − 4)(x + 2) [1]. So x = 1, x = 4 or x = −2 [1].
Let P(x) = x⁴ + x³ − 7x² − x + 6. Show that (x − 1) and (x + 1) are both factors of P(x), and hence factorise P(x) completely. (4 marks)
Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when P(x) = 6x³ − x² + 4x − 1 is divided by (2x − 1). (2 marks)
(2x + 1) is a factor of P(x) = 2x³ + 7x² + kx − 3. Find k and the quotient when P(x) is divided by (2x + 1). (3 marks)
P(−1/2) = −1/4 + 7/4 − k/2 − 3 = 0 [1], so −3/2 − k/2 = 0 and k = −3 [1]. Division gives P(x) = (2x + 1)(x² + 3x − 3), so the quotient is x² + 3x − 3 [1].
Use the factor theorem to determine whether (x + 2) is a factor of P(x) = x³ + 4x² − x − 6. (2 marks)

The volume of a box is V(x) = x³ + 3x² − 4x − 12 cm³, where x > 2. Show that (x + 3) is a factor of V(x), factorise V(x) completely to find expressions for the three dimensions of the box, and find the volume when x = 5. (4 marks)

V(−3) = −27 + 27 + 12 − 12 = 0, so (x + 3) is a factor [1]. Division gives V(x) = (x + 3)(x² − 4) [1] = (x + 3)(x − 2)(x + 2), so the dimensions are (x + 3), (x − 2) and (x + 2) cm [1]. When x = 5: 8 × 3 × 7 = 168 cm³ [1].
Find all real solutions of 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6 = 0. (3 marks)
Show that (x − 1) is a factor of P(x) = x³ − 5x² + 7x − 3 and hence factorise P(x) completely, stating which factor is repeated. (3 marks)
P(1) = 1 − 5 + 7 − 3 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor [1]. Division gives P(x) = (x − 1)(x² − 4x + 3) [1] = (x − 1)²(x − 3), so (x − 1) is the repeated factor [1].
When a polynomial P(x) is divided by (x − 3) the quotient is x² + 2x − 1 and the remainder is 4. Write down P(x) in expanded form and verify that P(3) = 4. (3 marks)
When P(x) = 2x³ + kx² − x + 4 is divided by (x + 1), the remainder is 7. What is the value of k?
By the remainder theorem P(−1) = −2 + k + 1 + 4 = k + 3 = 7, so k = 4. Evaluating P(1) instead gives the incorrect equation k + 5 = 7.
P(x) = x³ + ax² − 4x + 4 has (x − 2) as a factor. Find a, and the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x + 1).
vce-methods12-solving-polynomial-equatio: Which gives all the real solutions of x³ − 4x = 0?
x(x² − 4) = x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0, 2 or −2. Dividing both sides by x would lose the solution x = 0.
What is the solution set of x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0?
Let u = x²: u² − 13u + 36 = (u − 4)(u − 9) = 0, so x² = 4 or x² = 9, giving x = ±2 or ±3. The first option stops at u.
The equation 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6 = 0 has x = −2 as a solution. What is the sum of all its real solutions?
How many distinct real solutions does x³ − 6x² + 9x = 0 have?
x(x² − 6x + 9) = x(x − 3)² = 0, so x = 0 or x = 3. The repeated root counts once, so there are 2 distinct solutions.
How many real solutions does x³ + 8 = 0 have?
x³ + 8 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4). The quadratic has discriminant 4 − 16 < 0, so the only real solution is x = −2.
Solve (a) x⁴ − 10x² + 9 = 0 and (b) x⁴ + x² − 6 = 0 over R. (4 marks)
(a) Let u = x²: u² − 10u + 9 = (u − 1)(u − 9) = 0, so x² = 1 or 9, x = ±1 or ±3 [2]. (b) u² + u − 6 = (u + 3)(u − 2) = 0; x² = −3 has no real solution, x² = 2 gives x = ±√2 [2].
A rectangular box has dimensions x cm, (x + 2) cm and (x + 5) cm and volume 120 cm³. Form an equation in x and find the dimensions of the box. (4 marks)

x(x + 2)(x + 5) = 120, so x³ + 7x² + 10x − 120 = 0 [1]. Try x = 3: 27 + 63 + 30 − 120 = 0, so (x − 3) is a factor [1]. Dividing: (x − 3)(x² + 10x + 40) = 0; the quadratic has discriminant 100 − 160 < 0 so no further real roots [1]. x = 3, so the dimensions are 3 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm (3 × 5 × 8 = 120) [1].
Which gives all the solutions of (x − 1)(x + 4)(2x − 3) = 0?
Each factor is set to zero: x − 1 = 0, x + 4 = 0 and 2x − 3 = 0, giving x = 1, −4 and 3/2. Forgetting to divide by 2 in the last factor gives x = 3, which is wrong.
x(x² − 27) = 0, so x = 0 or x² = 27, giving x = ±3√3. Dividing through by x would lose x = 0, and x² = 27 does not give x = ±3.
The equation x³ − 2x² + kx − 6 = 0 has x = 2 as a solution. What is the value of k?
Substituting x = 2: 8 − 8 + 2k − 6 = 0, so 2k = 6 and k = 3. A sign error when moving the 6 across gives k = −3.
The equation x³ − 7x + 6 = 0 has solutions x = 1 and x = 2. What is its smallest real solution?
Dividing out (x − 1)(x − 2) = x² − 3x + 2 leaves (x + 3), so the third solution is x = −3. The solutions sum to 0 (there is no x² term), which also gives 1 + 2 + (−3) = 0.
What is the real solution of 2x³ − 16 = 0?
2x³ = 16 gives x³ = 8, so x = 2. A cube has only one real cube root, so x = −2 is not a solution; x = 8 forgets to take the cube root.
How many real solutions does x⁴ − 16 = 0 have?
x⁴ − 16 = (x² − 4)(x² + 4). The factor x² − 4 gives x = ±2, but x² + 4 = 0 has no real solution, so there are 2 real solutions, not 4.
How many distinct real solutions does x(x − 2)²(x + 1) = 0 have?
The solutions are x = 0, x = 2 (repeated) and x = −1. The repeated factor is counted once, so there are 3 distinct solutions, not 4.
By the rational root theorem, which of these cannot be a rational solution of 2x³ + x² − 5x + 3 = 0?
A rational solution p/q must have p dividing 3 and q dividing 2, so the candidates are ±1, ±3, ±1/2 and ±3/2. The value 2/3 has numerator 2, which does not divide 3.
Which gives the real solutions of x⁶ − 7x³ − 8 = 0?
Let u = x³: (u − 8)(u + 1) = 0, so x³ = 8 or x³ = −1, giving x = 2 or x = −1. Stopping at u gives 8 and −1, and cube roots have only one real value each, so there are no ± pairs.
The equation x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0 has three real solutions. What is their product?
For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 the product of the solutions is −d/a = −6. Using +6 forgets the negative sign in the formula.
Which gives all the solutions of x³ + 2x² = 3x?
x³ + 2x² − 3x = x(x² + 2x − 3) = x(x − 1)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 0, 1 or −3. Dividing both sides by x would lose x = 0.
Which gives all the real solutions of x⁴ − 5x² − 36 = 0?
Let u = x²: (u − 9)(u + 4) = 0, so x² = 9 or x² = −4. Only x² = 9 gives real solutions, x = ±3.
Which gives all the solutions of 2x³ + 3x² − 2x = 0?
x(2x² + 3x − 2) = x(2x − 1)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0, 1/2 or −2. The second option omits x = 0, and the others have sign errors in the quadratic factors.
Which equation has exactly the solutions x = 0, x = 2 and x = −3?
A solution x = a comes from the factor (x − a), so the factors are x, (x − 2) and (x + 3). Writing (x + 2) or (x − 3) reverses the sign of a solution.
How many real solutions does x³ + 4x = 0 have?
x(x² + 4) = 0. The factor x gives x = 0, while x² + 4 = 0 has no real solutions, so there is only 1 real solution.
What is the largest solution of x³ − 2x² − 8x = 0?
x(x² − 2x − 8) = x(x − 4)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0, 4 or −2 and the largest is 4. Reading the factor (x + 2) as x = 2 is a sign error.
Which gives all the real solutions of x³ + 3x² = 4?
Rearranging, x³ + 3x² − 4 = 0, and x = 1 works, giving (x − 1)(x² + 4x + 4) = (x − 1)(x + 2)². So x = 1 or x = −2 (a repeated solution).
Try x = 2: 8 + 8 − 10 − 6 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor [1]. Dividing gives (x − 2)(x² + 4x + 3) [1] = (x − 2)(x + 1)(x + 3), so x = 2, −1 or −3 [1].
Solve 2x³ − x² − 8x + 4 = 0 by factorising in pairs. (3 marks)
The equation x³ + kx² − 4x − 6 = 0 has x = −1 as a solution. Find k and hence find all real solutions. (4 marks)

Substitute x = −1: −1 + k + 4 − 6 = 0 [1], so k = 3 [1]. Dividing x³ + 3x² − 4x − 6 by (x + 1) gives (x + 1)(x² + 2x − 6) [1]. The quadratic gives x = −1 ± √7, so the solutions are x = −1, −1 + √7 and −1 − √7 [1].

A square sheet of cardboard with side length 12 cm has a square of side x cm cut from each corner. The sides are folded up to form an open box of volume 128 cm³. Show that x³ − 12x² + 36x − 32 = 0 and find the value of x. (4 marks)

The box has base (12 − 2x) by (12 − 2x) and height x, so x(12 − 2x)² = 128, giving 4x³ − 48x² + 144x − 128 = 0 and x³ − 12x² + 36x − 32 = 0 [1]. Try x = 2: 8 − 48 + 72 − 32 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor [1]. Dividing: (x − 2)(x² − 10x + 16) = (x − 2)(x − 2)(x − 8), so x = 2 or x = 8 [1]. Since 12 − 2x > 0 requires x < 6, x = 8 is rejected and x = 2 cm [1].
Try x = 1: 1 − 7 + 14 − 8 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor [1]. Dividing gives (x − 1)(x² − 6x + 8) [1] = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 4), so x = 1, 2 or 4 [1].
A student solves x³ = 4x² by dividing both sides by x² and writes x = 4. Identify the error and give the complete solution. (2 marks)
Dividing by x² assumes x ≠ 0, so the solution x = 0 is lost [1]. Correctly, x³ − 4x² = x²(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4 [1].
Which gives all the real solutions of (x² − 1)(x² + 4) = 0?
The factor x² + 4 is always positive, so only x² − 1 = 0 gives real solutions, x = ±1. The solutions ±2 would only occur if the factor were x² − 4.
What is the sum of the real solutions of x³ − 2x² − 15x = 0?
Factorising gives x(x − 5)(x + 3) = 0 with solutions 0, 5 and −3, which sum to 2. The value −2 comes from mis-signing the solutions (using −5 and 3).

A rectangular prism has a square base of side x cm and height (x + 2) cm. Its volume is 45 cm³. Form a cubic equation, show that x = 3 is a solution, and hence find the side length of the base. (4 marks)

x²(x + 2) = 45, so x³ + 2x² − 45 = 0 [1]. 27 + 18 − 45 = 0, so x = 3 is a solution [1]. x³ + 2x² − 45 = (x − 3)(x² + 5x + 15) and the discriminant 25 − 60 < 0, so no other real solutions [1]. The base has side 3 cm [1].
P(1) = 1 − 2 − 5 + 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor. Dividing gives x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2).
vce-methods12-power-functions-and-hyperb: What is the range of the function y = 1/x², x ≠ 0?
x² > 0 for x ≠ 0, so 1/x² > 0 and takes every positive value. It never equals 0 (asymptote), so the range is (0, ∞).
What are the equations of the asymptotes of y = 2/(x − 3) + 1?
The vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero (x = 3), and the horizontal asymptote is the vertical translation y = 1.
What is the x-intercept of y = 6/(x + 2) − 1?
Set 6/(x + 2) = 1, so x + 2 = 6 and x = 4. The value 2 is the y-intercept (3 − 1).
Which of these functions is an even function?
x⁻⁴ gives f(−x) = f(x), so it is symmetric about the y-axis. The other three satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) (odd).
For 0 < x < 1, which of the following has the greatest value?
For 0 < x < 1, a smaller index gives a larger value. For x = 0.25: x^(1/2) = 0.5, x^(3/2) = 0.125, x² = 0.0625, x³ ≈ 0.016.
For y = 3/(x − 1) + 2, find the equations of the asymptotes, the axis intercepts, the domain and the range. (4 marks)
Asymptotes: x = 1 and y = 2 [1]. y-intercept: 3/(−1) + 2 = −1, so (0, −1) [1]. x-intercept: 3/(x − 1) = −2, so x − 1 = −3/2 and x = −1/2, so (−1/2, 0) [1]. Domain R \ {1}, range R \ {2} [1].
Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of y = 4/x and y = x + 3. (3 marks)
A power function has the rule y = ax^n and passes through (1, 2) and (2, 16). Find a and n, and state whether the function is odd, even or neither. (3 marks)
What is the domain of the function y = 1/(x + 4) − 5?
The denominator is zero when x = −4, so x = −4 is excluded. The value −5 is the vertical translation, which affects the range, not the domain.
What is the range of the function y = 3/x − 2?
The horizontal asymptote is y = −2, and 3/x takes every non-zero value, so y takes every value except −2. Excluding 2 would come from misreading the sign of the translation.
In which quadrants does the graph of y = a/x lie when a < 0?
When a < 0, positive x gives negative y (fourth quadrant) and negative x gives positive y (second quadrant). First and third quadrants is the case for a > 0.
Which of the following power functions has domain R and is an even function?
x^(2/3) = (∛x)² is defined for all real x and satisfies f(−x) = f(x). Although x⁻² is even, it is undefined at x = 0, so its domain is not R.
What is the domain of the function y = x^(1/2)?
x^(1/2) = √x requires x ≥ 0, and x = 0 gives a valid output of 0. The interval (0, ∞) wrongly excludes x = 0.
A hyperbola has asymptotes x = 2 and y = −1 and passes through (0, 1). Which is its equation?
Write y = a/(x − 2) − 1 and substitute (0, 1): 1 = −a/2 − 1, so a = −4. The positive version gives y = −3 at x = 0.
How many points of intersection do the graphs of y = 1/x and y = −x have?
Setting 1/x = −x gives x² = −1, which has no real solution. Students who forget the sign and solve x² = 1 would wrongly find two points.
The graph of y = 1/x is dilated by a factor of 3 from the y-axis. What is the equation of the image?
A dilation by factor 3 from the y-axis replaces x with x/3, giving y = 1/(x/3) = 3/x. The rule 1/(3x) corresponds to a dilation by factor 1/3 from the y-axis.
For the graph of y = 1/x, what happens to y as x approaches 0 from the left (x → 0⁻)?
For small negative x, 1/x is a large negative number, so y → −∞. The behaviour y → ∞ occurs as x approaches 0 from the right.
8^(−2/3) = 1/(8^(1/3))² = 1/2² = 1/4. A negative index gives a reciprocal, not a negative value.
What are all the real solutions of x^(2/3) = 4?
x^(2/3) = (∛x)² = 4 gives ∛x = ±2, so x = ±8. Giving only x = 8 misses the negative solution, which also works since (−8)^(2/3) = 4.
At which points do the graphs of y = x^(1/2) and y = x^(1/3) intersect?
Solving x^(1/2) = x^(1/3) gives x^(1/3)(x^(1/6) − 1) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 1. The point (−1, −1) is not on y = x^(1/2), which is undefined for negative x.
Which statement about the function f(x) = 1/x is correct?
Swapping x and y in y = 1/x gives x = 1/y, so y = 1/x; the graph is symmetric about y = x. It is one-to-one, so an inverse exists, and it is not −1/x.
Which of the following is equal to y = (3x − 5)/(x − 1)?
Since 3x − 5 = 3(x − 1) − 2, the expression equals 3 − 2/(x − 1). The positive 2/(x − 1) version results from a sign error.
What is the y-coordinate of the point on y = −8/x where x = −2?
y = −8/(−2) = 4. A negative divided by a negative is positive, so −4 is incorrect.
What is the range of y = 1/(x − 2)² + 3?
1/(x − 2)² is always positive and never zero, so y > 3 and the range is (3, ∞). The interval [3, ∞) is wrong because y = 3 is only approached, never reached.
A hyperbola with rule y = a/x passes through (−3, 4). Which is its rule?
Substituting gives 4 = a/(−3), so a = −12. Using a = 12 ignores that x is negative.
State the equations of the asymptotes, the domain and the range of y = −2/(x + 1) + 4. (3 marks)
Asymptotes: x = −1 and y = 4 [1]. Domain: R \ {−1} [1]. Range: R \ {4} [1].
A hyperbola has asymptotes x = 1 and y = 3 and passes through the point (3, 5). Find its equation. (3 marks)
Show that y = x⁻³ is an odd function, and state its domain. (2 marks)
f(−x) = (−x)⁻³ = −x⁻³ = −f(x), so the function is odd [1]. Domain: R \ {0} [1].
Express y = (2x + 5)/(x + 1) in the form y = a/(x − h) + k, and hence state the equations of the asymptotes and the y-intercept. (3 marks)
2x + 5 = 2(x + 1) + 3, so y = 3/(x + 1) + 2 [1]. Asymptotes: x = −1 and y = 2 [1]. y-intercept: when x = 0, y = 5, so (0, 5) [1].
Evaluate 16^(3/4) and 125^(−2/3), giving exact values. (2 marks)
Describe, in order, a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of y = 1/x onto the graph of y = −2/(x + 3) + 1. (3 marks)
Dilation by a factor of 2 from the x-axis (y = 2/x) [1]. Reflection in the x-axis (y = −2/x) [1]. Translation 3 units to the left and 1 unit up [1].

The time T hours to fill a tank is inversely proportional to the number of pumps n, so T = k/n. With 4 pumps the tank fills in 6 hours. Find k, the time taken by 8 pumps, and the number of pumps needed to fill the tank in 2 hours. (3 marks)
6 = k/4, so k = 24 [1]. With 8 pumps, T = 24/8 = 3 hours [1]. 24/n = 2, so n = 12 pumps [1].
Find the points where the graphs of y = x⁻² and y = x⁻⁴ intersect, and state which graph is higher when |x| > 1. (3 marks)
x⁻² = x⁻⁴ gives x⁴ = x², so x²(x² − 1) = 0 and x = ±1 (x ≠ 0) [1]. Points: (1, 1) and (−1, 1) [1]. For |x| > 1, x⁻² > x⁻⁴ (e.g. x = 2: 1/4 > 1/16), so y = x⁻² is higher [1].
Find the rule for the inverse of f(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, and state its domain and range. (3 marks)
Swap x and y: x = 1/(y − 2) + 3 [1]. Rearrange: y − 2 = 1/(x − 3), so f⁻¹(x) = 1/(x − 3) + 2 [1]. Domain R \ {3}, range R \ {2} [1].
What is the y-intercept of y = 4/(x − 2) + 1?
At x = 0, y = 4/(−2) + 1 = −1. Mistakenly using x + 2 in the denominator would give the incorrect 3.
What is the range of y = 2 − 3x^(1/3)?
The cube root function has domain R and range R, and scaling by −3 and shifting up by 2 keeps the range as all real numbers. The restriction y ≤ 2 would apply to a square root, not a cube root.
Let f(x) = −1/(x − 3)² + 2. State the equations of the asymptotes, the domain, the range and the x-intercepts of f. (4 marks)
Asymptotes x = 3 and y = 2 [1]. Domain R \ {3} [1]. Range (−∞, 2) [1]. Solving 1/(x − 3)² = 2 gives (x − 3)² = 1/2, so x = 3 ± √2/2 [1].
A power function has rule y = kx⁻² and passes through (3, 2). Find k and the value of y when x = −6, and explain why the graph is symmetrical about the y-axis. (3 marks)
2 = k/9 so k = 18 [1]. y = 18/36 = 1/2 when x = −6 [1]. f(−x) = 18/(−x)² = f(x), so the function is even and symmetrical about the y-axis [1].
For y = 2/(x − 1) + 3, the asymptotes and x-intercept are:
vce-methods12-transformations-of-graphs: The graph of y = x² is reflected in the x-axis, then translated 3 units to the right and 2 units up. What is the equation of the image?
Reflection in the x-axis gives y = −x². Moving 3 right replaces x with x − 3, and 2 up adds 2: y = −(x − 3)² + 2.
The point (2, 5) lies on y = f(x). What is the corresponding point on the graph of y = 2f(x + 1) − 3?
x + 1 = 2 gives x = 1 (a shift of 1 to the left, not right). The y-value becomes 2(5) − 3 = 7. The image point is (1, 7).
How is the graph of y = f(3x) obtained from the graph of y = f(x)?
Dilation by factor 3 from the y-axis
Dilation by factor 3 from the x-axis
Dilation by factor 1/3 from the x-axis
Dilation by factor 1/3 from the y-axis
Replacing x with 3x compresses the graph horizontally by a factor of 1/3, that is a dilation of factor 1/3 from the y-axis (parallel to the x-axis).
The graph of y = 1/x is dilated by a factor of 3 from the x-axis, reflected in the y-axis, then translated 1 unit up. What is the equation of the image?
Dilation: y = 3/x. Reflection in the y-axis replaces x with −x: y = −3/x. Translation up 1: y = −3/x + 1.
What is the range of y = −√(4 − x) + 1?
√(4 − x) ≥ 0, so −√(4 − x) ≤ 0 and y ≤ 1. The range is (−∞, 1]. (−∞, 4] is the domain.
Describe a sequence of transformations that maps y = x² onto y = −2(x + 1)² + 5, and state the coordinates of the vertex and the y-intercept of the image. (3 marks)
Dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, reflection in the x-axis, translation 1 unit left and 5 units up [1]. Vertex (−1, 5) [1]. y-intercept: −2(1) + 5 = 3, so (0, 3) [1].
The points (−3, 4), (0, 0) and (2, −1) lie on y = f(x). Find the corresponding points on y = −f(x − 1) + 2. (3 marks)

The graph of y = x³ − x is dilated by a factor of 2 from the x-axis and then reflected in the y-axis. (a) Find the equation of the image. (b) The point (2, 6) is on the original graph. Find its image. (4 marks)

(a) Dilation gives y = 2(x³ − x) [1]; reflection in the y-axis replaces x with −x: y = 2(−x³ + x) = −2x³ + 2x [1]. (b) (x, y) → (−x, 2y), so (2, 6) → (−2, 12) [1]. Check: −2(−8) + 2(−2) = 16 − 4 = 12 [1].
The graph of y = x² is translated 5 units to the left. What is the equation of the image?
Moving left by 5 replaces x with x + 5, giving y = (x + 5)². y = (x − 5)² would be a shift to the right.
Which equation gives the reflection of y = f(x) in the x-axis?
Reflection in the x-axis changes the sign of every y-value, so y = −f(x). y = f(−x) is the reflection in the y-axis.
The point (6, −2) lies on y = f(x). What is the corresponding point on y = f(x/3)?
x/3 = 6 gives x = 18, so the graph is stretched horizontally by factor 3 and the y-value is unchanged. (2, −2) would come from f(3x).
What is the domain of y = √(x + 3) − 2?
We need x + 3 ≥ 0, so x ≥ −3. The −2 shifts the range, not the domain.
What is the range of y = −3(x + 2)² + 4?
The parabola opens downwards (negative coefficient) with vertex (−2, 4), so y ≤ 4. [4, ∞) would be the range if it opened upwards.
What are the asymptotes of y = 1/(x − 2) + 3?
The graph of y = 1/x is translated 2 right and 3 up, so the asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0 move to x = 2 and y = 3. x = −2 would result from a shift to the left.
The line y = 2x + 1 is reflected in the y-axis. What is the equation of the image?
Replace x with −x: y = −2x + 1. y = −2x − 1 is the reflection in the x-axis.
The graph of y = f(x) has x-intercepts at x = −2 and x = 4. Where are the x-intercepts of y = f(2x)?
f(2x) = 0 when 2x = −2 or 4, so x = −1 or 2. The graph is compressed horizontally by factor 1/2; x = −4 and 8 would come from f(x/2).
The graph of y = x² is translated 4 units up and then reflected in the x-axis. What is the equation of the image?
Translating up gives y = x² + 4. Reflecting in the x-axis negates the whole expression: y = −(x² + 4) = −x² − 4. Reflecting first would give −x² + 4.
The graph of y = x² + 2x is translated 2 units to the right. What is the equation of the image?
Replace x with x − 2: (x − 2)² + 2(x − 2) = x² − 4x + 4 + 2x − 4 = x² − 2x. Using x + 2 would give x² + 6x + 8.
The graph of y = x² − 4 is dilated by factor 3 from the y-axis. What are the x-intercepts of the image?
The image is y = (x/3)² − 4. Setting it to 0 gives x² = 36, so x = ±6. Each x-intercept is multiplied by 3.
If f(x) = x², what is the y-intercept of y = 2f(x − 1) + 3?
At x = 0: 2f(−1) + 3 = 2(1) + 3 = 5. Using f(0) = 0 would incorrectly give 3.
The function f has domain [−1, 5]. What is the domain of y = f(x − 3)?
We need −1 ≤ x − 3 ≤ 5, so 2 ≤ x ≤ 8. The graph shifts 3 units right, so the domain shifts right as well.
The function f has range [−2, 6]. What is the range of y = −f(x) + 1?
−f has range [−6, 2], and adding 1 gives [−5, 3]. The reflection reverses the order of the endpoints, so [−1, 7] is wrong.
Which sequence of translations maps y = x² onto y = x² − 6x + 11?
Completing the square gives y = (x − 3)² + 2. This is a translation of 3 right and 2 up; 11 is not the vertical shift.
The graph of y = √x is reflected in the y-axis and then translated 2 units to the right. What is the equation of the image?
Reflection gives y = √(−x). Replacing x with x − 2 gives y = √(−(x − 2)) = √(2 − x). √(−x − 2) would come from translating first.
A parabola is obtained from y = x² by a dilation from the x-axis and translations, has vertex (1, −2) and passes through (3, 6). What is its equation?
Write y = a(x − 1)² − 2. At x = 3: 4a − 2 = 6, so a = 2. The vertex (1, −2) gives (x − 1), not (x + 1).
The graph of y = x³ + x² is reflected in the y-axis. What is the equation of the image?
Replace x with −x: (−x)³ + (−x)² = −x³ + x². Only the odd-power term changes sign.
Express y = x² − 4x + 1 in turning point form and describe the translation that maps y = x² onto it. (2 marks)
y = (x − 2)² − 3 [1]. Translation 2 units right and 3 units down, so the vertex is (2, −3) [1].
The graph of y = 1/x is dilated by factor 2 from the x-axis, translated 1 unit left and 3 units down. Find the equation of the image, its asymptotes and its axis intercepts. (3 marks)
Equation y = 2/(x + 1) − 3 [1]. Asymptotes x = −1 and y = −3 [1]. y-intercept 2 − 3 = −1, so (0, −1); x-intercept 2/(x + 1) = 3 gives x = −1/3, so (−1/3, 0) [1].
The point (4, −6) lies on y = f(x). Find the corresponding point on y = 3f(x/2) + 1. (2 marks)
x/2 = 4 gives x = 8 [1]. y = 3(−6) + 1 = −17, so the image point is (8, −17) [1].
The graph of y = x² is translated 2 units left, dilated by factor 3 from the x-axis, then reflected in the x-axis. Find the equation of the image, its vertex and its y-intercept. (3 marks)
Translation: y = (x + 2)²; dilation: y = 3(x + 2)²; reflection: y = −3(x + 2)² [1]. Vertex (−2, 0) [1]. y-intercept: −3(2)² = −12, so (0, −12) [1].

The graph of f(x) = √x is dilated by factor 4 from the y-axis, reflected in the x-axis, then translated 3 units up to give g. Find the equation of g, its domain and range, and its x-intercept. (4 marks)
The graph of y = −(x + 3)² + 6 is obtained from y = x². Describe the transformations, state the vertex, and find the x-intercepts. (3 marks)
Reflection in the x-axis, translation 3 units left and 6 units up [1]. Vertex (−3, 6) [1]. (x + 3)² = 6 gives x = −3 ± √6 [1].
The line y = 3x − 2 is translated 4 units right and 1 unit down. Find the equation of the image. (2 marks)
Replace x with x − 4 and subtract 1: y = 3(x − 4) − 2 − 1 [1]. y = 3x − 15 [1].
A parabola has vertex (−1, 3) and passes through (1, −5). Find its equation and describe how it is obtained from y = x². (3 marks)
y = a(x + 1)² + 3 [1]. At x = 1: 4a + 3 = −5, so a = −2 and y = −2(x + 1)² + 3 [1]. Dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, reflection in the x-axis, translation 1 unit left and 3 units up [1].
(a) Write y = 4x² + 8x + 3 in the form y = a(x − h)² + k. (b) Describe the transformations from y = x². (c) Find the x-intercepts. (4 marks)
(a) y = 4(x + 1)² − 1 [1]. (b) Dilation by factor 4 from the x-axis, translation 1 unit left and 1 unit down [1]. (c) 4(x + 1)² = 1 gives (x + 1)² = 1/4 [1], so x = −1/2 and x = −3/2 [1].
The graph of y = f(x) has x-intercepts at −1 and 5 and a maximum turning point at (2, 9). For y = 2f(x + 1), find the x-intercepts and the turning point, and state its nature. (3 marks)
Each point (x, y) maps to (x − 1, 2y). x-intercepts (−2, 0) and (4, 0) [1]. Turning point (1, 18) [1]. It is still a maximum since the dilation factor is positive [1].
The point (4, −1) is a turning point of y = f(x). What is the corresponding turning point of y = f(2x − 6)?
Solving 2x − 6 = 4 gives x = 5, and the y-value is unchanged. Computing (4 − 6)/2 or 2(4) − 6 applies the transformation in the wrong direction.
The point (1, 3) lies on y = f(x). What is the corresponding point on y = −f(x + 2) − 1?
The x-value shifts 2 units left to −1, and the y-value becomes −3 − 1 = −4. Shifting right instead of left would give the incorrect x-value 3.

The graph of y = 1/x² is dilated by a factor of 2 from the y-axis, reflected in the x-axis, then translated 1 unit right and 4 units up. Find the equation of the final image, and state its asymptotes and range. (4 marks)
Dilation from the y-axis replaces x with x/2, giving y = 4/x² [1]. Reflection and translation give y = −4/(x − 1)² + 4 [1]. Asymptotes x = 1 and y = 4 [1]. Range (−∞, 4) [1].
The graph of y = x² is dilated by a factor of 2 from the y-axis, then translated 3 units to the left. Its new equation is:
Dilation from the y-axis by 2 replaces x with x/2. Translating left 3 then replaces x with x + 3: ((x + 3)/2)². Order matters.
vce-methods12-inverse-functions: What is the inverse of the function f(x) = 3x − 6?
Swap and solve: x = 3y − 6, so y = (x + 6)/3. The first option adds in the wrong order (undoing the operations out of sequence).
Let f(x) = (x − 2)² + 1, with domain [2, ∞). What is the range of f⁻¹?
The range of f⁻¹ equals the domain of f, which is [2, ∞). The set [1, ∞) is the range of f (and domain of f⁻¹).
Which function has an inverse function over its maximal domain R?
An inverse function exists only if f is one-to-one. y = x³ + 1 passes the horizontal line test; the other three are even, so each output is hit twice.
The graphs of f(x) = 2x − 3 and f⁻¹ intersect at which point?
The graphs of f and f⁻¹ are reflections in y = x, so they meet where f(x) = x: 2x − 3 = x gives x = 3, point (3, 3).
Let f(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3. What is the equation of the vertical asymptote of f⁻¹?
f has horizontal asymptote y = 3. Reflecting in y = x swaps x and y, so f⁻¹(x) = 1/(x − 3) + 2 has vertical asymptote x = 3.
Let f(x) = √(x + 3) − 1. Find the domain and range of f, the rule for f⁻¹, and the domain of f⁻¹. (4 marks)

Domain of f: x + 3 ≥ 0, so [−3, ∞); range [−1, ∞) [1]. Swap: x = √(y + 3) − 1, so √(y + 3) = x + 1 and y = (x + 1)² − 3 [1]. f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)² − 3 [1], with domain equal to the range of f, [−1, ∞) [1].
Let f(x) = x² − 4x + 1. (a) Find the largest domain of the form [a, ∞) for which f has an inverse. (b) Find f⁻¹ for that domain and state its domain. (4 marks)

(a) f(x) = (x − 2)² − 3 has its turning point at x = 2, so the largest such domain is [2, ∞) [1]. (b) x = (y − 2)² − 3, so y − 2 = √(x + 3) (positive root since y ≥ 2) [1]; f⁻¹(x) = 2 + √(x + 3) [1]; domain [−3, ∞) [1]. Check: f(5) = 6 and f⁻¹(6) = 2 + 3 = 5.
Let f(x) = (x + 3)/(x − 1), x ≠ 1. Show that f is its own inverse. (3 marks)
A function f is one-to-one and f(4) = 9. What is f⁻¹(9)?
An inverse reverses the mapping, so f⁻¹(9) = 4. The value 1/4 confuses an inverse function with a reciprocal.
A function has an inverse function if and only if it is
Each output must come from exactly one input, which is the one-to-one (horizontal line) test. Continuity is not enough: y = x² is continuous but has no inverse function over R.
What is the inverse of f(x) = x³ − 8?
Swap and solve: x = y³ − 8, so y³ = x + 8 and y = ∛(x + 8). The option ∛(x − 8) takes the cube root without first adding 8.
The graph of y = f(x) passes through (2, 5). Which point must lie on the graph of y = f⁻¹(x)?
Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates, so (2, 5) becomes (5, 2). Taking reciprocals of the coordinates is a common confusion between inverse and reciprocal.
Let f(x) = x², with domain (−∞, 0]. What is the rule for f⁻¹?
The range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f, (−∞, 0], so only the negative root is allowed: f⁻¹(x) = −√x. The positive root would give outputs that are not in (−∞, 0].
What is the largest domain of the form (−∞, a] on which f(x) = (x + 1)² − 4 has an inverse?
The turning point is at x = −1, so f is one-to-one on (−∞, −1]. The value −4 is the y-coordinate of the turning point, not its x-coordinate.
Let f(x) = √(x − 1) + 2. What is the domain of f⁻¹?
The domain of f⁻¹ equals the range of f. Since √(x − 1) ≥ 0, the range of f is [2, ∞). The set [1, ∞) is the domain of f.
Let g(x) = 3ˣ. What is the rule for g⁻¹?
Swapping gives x = 3ʸ, which by definition means y = log₃(x). Raising x to the power 3 is a different operation, and 1/3ˣ is the reflection in the y-axis, not in y = x.
Let f(x) = 4 − x. Which statement is true?
Swapping gives x = 4 − y, so y = 4 − x. The function is its own inverse, since f(f(x)) = 4 − (4 − x) = x.
Let f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 2), x ≠ −2. What is the equation of the horizontal asymptote of f⁻¹?
Solving x = (y − 1)/(y + 2) gives f⁻¹(x) = (−2x − 1)/(x − 1), which has horizontal asymptote y = −2. The vertical asymptote of f (x = −2) becomes the horizontal asymptote of f⁻¹.
Let f(x) = x² + 6x with domain [−3, ∞). What is the rule for f⁻¹?
Completing the square gives f(x) = (x + 3)² − 9, so x = (y + 3)² − 9 and y = −3 ± √(x + 9). Since y ≥ −3, the positive root is used.
Let f(x) = 3x + 1. What is the value of f⁻¹(10)?
f⁻¹(x) = (x − 1)/3, so f⁻¹(10) = 9/3 = 3. The value 31 is f(10), which applies f instead of f⁻¹.
Which pair of functions are inverses of each other?
Inverses satisfy f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) = x. Here (x − 4) + 4 = x and (x + 4) − 4 = x. In the pair 3x and −3x, the composite is −9x, not x.
A one-to-one function f has domain [−2, 5] and range [1, 9]. What is the domain of f⁻¹?
The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, so it is [1, 9]. The set [−2, 5] is the range of f⁻¹.
How many points of intersection do the graphs of y = x³ and its inverse have?
Since x³ is increasing, the graphs meet where x³ = x, giving x = −1, 0 and 1, so three points. Many students find only x = 1 or x = 0 and miss the others.
Let f(x) = √x, x ≥ 0. Which description of f⁻¹ is correct?
Swapping gives x = √y, so y = x², and the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, which is x ≥ 0. Leaving the domain as R would make f⁻¹ not match the reflection of f.
Let f(x) = 5 − 2x. Find the rule for f⁻¹ and state its domain and range. (3 marks)
Swap and solve: x = 5 − 2y, so y = (5 − x)/2, giving f⁻¹(x) = (5 − x)/2 [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ is R [1]. Range of f⁻¹ is R [1].
Let f(x) = 2/(x + 1) − 3, x ≠ −1. Find the rule for f⁻¹ and state its domain and range. (4 marks)
Swap: x = 2/(y + 1) − 3, so x + 3 = 2/(y + 1) [1]. Then y + 1 = 2/(x + 3), so f⁻¹(x) = 2/(x + 3) − 1 [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = R \ {−3} [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = R \ {−1} [1].
Let g(x) = 3x − 7 and h(x) = (x + 7)/3. Show that h is the inverse of g. (2 marks)
Let f(x) = (x + 1)² − 5, x ≤ −1. Find f⁻¹, stating its domain and range. (4 marks)
Swap: x = (y + 1)² − 5, so (y + 1)² = x + 5 [1]. Since y ≤ −1, y + 1 = −√(x + 5), so f⁻¹(x) = −1 − √(x + 5) [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = [−5, ∞) [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = (−∞, −1] [1].
Let f(x) = √(2x + 3), x ≥ −3/2. Find f⁻¹ and its domain, then find the coordinates of the point where the graphs of f and f⁻¹ intersect. (4 marks)

Swap: x = √(2y + 3), so x² = 2y + 3 and f⁻¹(x) = (x² − 3)/2 [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = [0, ∞) [1]. Intersection lies on y = x: √(2x + 3) = x, so 2x + 3 = x², i.e. (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0 [1]. x = −1 is rejected since √1 ≠ −1, so the point is (3, 3) [1].
Let f(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. Find the rule for f⁻¹, and state the domain and range of f⁻¹. (4 marks)
Swap: x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2), so xy − 2x = 3y + 1 [1]. Then y(x − 3) = 2x + 1, so f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = R \ {3} [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = R \ {2} [1].
Explain, using the horizontal line test, why f(x) = x² − 4 with domain R has no inverse function. State a restricted domain on which an inverse does exist. (3 marks)

A horizontal line such as y = 0 cuts the graph at two points [1], so f is not one-to-one, e.g. f(−2) = f(2) = 0 [1]. Restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 (or x ≤ 0) makes f one-to-one, so an inverse exists [1].
Let f(x) = 2ˣ + 1. Find the rule for f⁻¹ and state its domain and range. (3 marks)
Swap: x = 2ʸ + 1, so 2ʸ = x − 1 and f⁻¹(x) = log₂(x − 1) [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = (1, ∞) [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = R [1].
Let f(x) = (x − 1)³ + 2. Find f⁻¹(x), and hence evaluate f⁻¹(10). (3 marks)
Let f(x) = |x − 3| + 1, x ≤ 3. Find the rule for f⁻¹, and state its domain and range. (4 marks)
For x ≤ 3, |x − 3| = 3 − x, so f(x) = 4 − x [1]. Swap: x = 4 − y, so f⁻¹(x) = 4 − x [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = [1, ∞) [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = (−∞, 3] [1].
The temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is given by F = 1.8C + 32, where C is the temperature in °C. Find the inverse rule giving C in terms of F, and use it to convert 86°F to °C. (3 marks)
Let f(x) = −√(4 − x), x ≤ 4. Find f⁻¹, stating its domain and range. (4 marks)
Swap: x = −√(4 − y), so x² = 4 − y [1]. f⁻¹(x) = 4 − x² [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f = (−∞, 0] [1]. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f = (−∞, 4] [1].
Let f(x) = (2x + 1)/3. What is the rule for f⁻¹?
Swapping gives x = (2y + 1)/3, so y = (3x − 1)/2. Taking the reciprocal is not the same as finding an inverse function.
Let f(x) = x² + 2 with domain [0, ∞). What is the value of f⁻¹(11)?
Solving x² + 2 = 11 gives x² = 9, and the domain restriction means x = 3 only. The value −3 is not in the domain of f.
Let f(x) = x² + 4x, x ≥ −2. Find f⁻¹, stating its domain, and find the coordinates of the point where f and f⁻¹ intersect. (4 marks)

f(x) = (x + 2)² − 4 so f⁻¹(x) = √(x + 4) − 2 [1]. Domain of f⁻¹ is [−4, ∞) (the range of f) [1]. Solve f(x) = x: x² + 3x = 0 so x = 0 or x = −3 [1]. x = −3 is outside the domain, so the intersection is (0, 0) [1].
f(x) = (x − 1)² + 2 with domain x ≥ 1. Its inverse is:
Swap x and y: x = (y − 1)² + 2, so y = 1 ± √(x − 2). The range of f is y ≥ 1, so take the positive root. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f: x ≥ 2.
vce-methods12-index-laws: Simplify (2x³y⁻²)³ ÷ (4x⁴y⁻³), writing the answer with positive indices.
(2x³y⁻²)³ = 8x⁹y⁻⁶. Dividing by 4x⁴y⁻³ gives 2x⁵y⁻³ = 2x⁵/y³. The y index is −6 − (−3) = −3, not −9 or +3.
27^(−2/3) = 1/(27^(1/3))² = 1/3² = 1/9. A negative index gives a reciprocal, not a negative number.
8^(x+1) can be written as a power of 2 as
8 = 2³, so 8^(x+1) = 2^(3(x+1)) = 2^(3x+3). The index 3 multiplies the whole exponent (x + 1), not just x.
√48 = 4√3 and √12 = 2√3, so the difference is 2√3. Surds cannot be subtracted as √(48 − 12) = √36.
Write both sides with base 3: 3^(2x) = 3^(3(x − 1)) = 3^(3x − 3); equate indices: 2x = 3x − 3; x = 3 (check: 9³ = 729 = 27²).
Simplify (a^(1/2) b⁻¹)⁴ × (a^(3/2) b²)⁻², giving your answer with positive indices. (3 marks)
(a^(1/2) b⁻¹)⁴ = a²b⁻⁴; (a^(3/2) b²)⁻² = a⁻³b⁻⁴; product = a^(2 − 3) b^(−4 − 4) = a⁻¹b⁻⁸ = 1/(a b⁸).
Common denominator: [(2 − √3) + (2 + √3)] / [(2 + √3)(2 − √3)]; numerator = 4; denominator = 4 − 3 = 1; so the sum = 4/1 = 4.
Raising a power to a power multiplies the indices: 3 × 4 = 12. Adding the indices gives a⁷, which is the rule for multiplying.
5⁰ = 1 and 5⁻¹ = 1/5, so the sum is 6/5. Treating 5⁰ as 0 would give 1/5.
16^(3/4) = (16^(1/4))³ = 2³ = 8. Multiplying 16 by 3/4 to get 12 is not an index law.
Simplify (x⁵ × x⁻²) ÷ x⁴, writing the answer with a positive index.
The index is 5 − 2 − 4 = −1, so the result is x⁻¹ = 1/x. Forgetting to subtract the divisor's index gives x³.
Multiplying powers with the same base adds indices: x + (x + 1) = 2x + 1. The base stays 2; it is not multiplied to 4.
√75 = √(25 × 3) = 5√3. The perfect square 25 comes out as its square root 5, not 25.
3√2 × 4√6 = 12√12 = 12 × 2√3 = 24√3. Adding the coefficients and radicands is incorrect for multiplication.
Writing both sides in base 2: 2^(2x) = 2⁻³, so 2x = −3 and x = −3/2. Dividing by the wrong index gives −2/3.
25 = 5², so 2x − 1 = 2 and x = 3/2. Setting 2x = 2 forgets the −1.
A negative index inverts the fraction: (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. It does not make the value negative.
Adding the indices gives 1/2 + 3/2 = 2, so the product is 5² = 25. Multiplying the indices would give 5^(3/4).
∛(x²) written with a fractional index is
The cube root gives denominator 3 and the square gives numerator 2, so x^(2/3). The reciprocal 3/2 reverses the roles.
The difference of two squares gives 3² − (√2)² = 9 − 2 = 7. Adding 9 and 2 gives 11, which ignores the negative sign.
2^(x+2) = 2ˣ × 2² = 5 × 4 = 20. Adding 2 to 5 treats an index as a term.
6 ÷ 3 = 2, a⁴⁻² = a², and b⁻¹⁻⁽⁻³⁾ = b². Adding the b indices instead gives b⁻⁴.
Expanding gives x + 2·x^(1/2)·x^(−1/2) + x⁻¹ = x + 2 + 1/x. Dropping the middle term is the common error of squaring each part only.
2⁻³ = 1/8 and 4² = 16, so the product is 2. Reading 2⁻³ as −8 gives −128 instead.
Simplify (3x²y⁻¹)² × (x⁻³y)³, writing the answer with positive indices. (3 marks)
Evaluate 27^(2/3) − 16^(−1/2), giving an exact fraction. (2 marks)
Let u = 2ˣ so u² − 5u + 4 = 0 [1]; (u − 1)(u − 4) = 0 so u = 1 or u = 4 [1]; 2ˣ = 1 gives x = 0 [1]; 2ˣ = 4 gives x = 2 [1].
Simplify (√2)⁵ ÷ 2^(−1/2) and give its value. (2 marks)
Express 10/(3 − √5) in the form (a + b√5)/c with a, b, c positive integers and c as small as possible. (3 marks)
Multiply top and bottom by (3 + √5) [1]; denominator = 9 − 5 = 4 [1]; 10(3 + √5)/4 = (15 + 5√5)/2 [1].
Given 2ˣ = a, write 4ˣ + 2^(x+1) in terms of a. (2 marks)
4ˣ = (2ˣ)² = a² [1]; 2^(x+1) = 2 × 2ˣ = 2a, so the expression is a² + 2a [1].
Simplify (8a³)^(2/3) ÷ (a^(1/2))², giving your answer in simplest form. (3 marks)
Find integers a and b such that (2 + √3)/(2 − √3) = a + b√3. (3 marks)
Multiply top and bottom by (2 + √3) [1]; denominator = 4 − 3 = 1 [1]; numerator (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3, so a = 7, b = 4 [1].
Written as a single power of 3, 9^(x − 1) ÷ 27^x equals
9^(x − 1) = 3^(2x − 2) and 27^x = 3^(3x), so dividing gives 3^(2x − 2 − 3x) = 3^(−x − 2). Adding the indices would suit multiplication, not division.
Multiplying top and bottom by √6 gives 4√6/6 = 2√6/3. Forgetting to divide by the new denominator 6 gives the incorrect 4√6.
Multiply top and bottom by (√5 + √2) [1]. Numerator (√5 + √2)² = 5 + 2√10 + 2 = 7 + 2√10 [1]. Denominator 5 − 2 = 3 [1].
(27a⁶b³)^(1/3) = 3a²b and (9a²)^(1/2) = 3a, so the quotient is ab.
vce-methods12-exponential-graphs: The graph of y = 2^x is translated 3 units to the right and 1 unit up. The equation of the image is
Translating right by 3 replaces x by (x − 3); translating up by 1 adds 1. So y = 2^(x − 3) + 1.
Which statement about f(x) = (1/2)^x is correct?
It is strictly increasing with asymptote y = 0.
It is strictly decreasing with y-intercept (0, 1/2).
It is strictly increasing with y-intercept (0, 1).
It is strictly decreasing with horizontal asymptote y = 0.
Since 0 < 1/2 < 1 the function is decreasing; f(0) = 1; f(x) → 0 as x → ∞, so y = 0 is the asymptote.
The graph of f(x) = a × b^x, where b > 0, passes through (1, 6) and (3, 54). The values of a and b are
Dividing: ab³/(ab) = b² = 54/6 = 9, so b = 3 (b > 0). Then 3a = 6 gives a = 2.
2^x > 0 for all x, so −2^x < 0 and f(x) < 5. f takes every value below 5, so the range is (−∞, 5).
Let f(x) = 2^(x + 1) − 8. (a) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote. (b) Find the y-intercept. (c) Find the x-intercept. (d) State the range. (4 marks)
Describe, in order, a sequence of transformations that maps y = 2^x to y = −2^(x − 1) + 3. Hence state the asymptote and y-intercept of the image. (3 marks)
Translate 1 unit right, reflect in the x-axis, translate 3 units up; asymptote y = 3; y-intercept: −2⁻¹ + 3 = 5/2, i.e. (0, 2.5).
The graph of y = a × 2^x + c has horizontal asymptote y = −2 and passes through (0, 1). Find a and c, and find y when x = 2. (3 marks)
Asymptote gives c = −2; at x = 0: a + c = 1 so a = 3; rule y = 3 × 2^x − 2; at x = 2: y = 3 × 4 − 2 = 10.
Which point lies on the graph of y = 5^x?
5⁻¹ = 1/5, so (−1, 1/5) lies on the graph. The y-value at x = −1 is positive, so (−1, −5) is wrong.
The horizontal asymptote of the graph of y = 2^(x − 3) + 5 is
Horizontal translation does not move a horizontal asymptote; the 2^(x − 3) part tends to 0, so y → 5. The 3 only shifts the graph right.
The graph of y = 3^x is reflected in the y-axis. The equation of the image is
Reflection in the y-axis replaces x by −x, giving y = 3^(−x). Reflection in the x-axis would give y = −3^x.
4^x > 0 for all x, so f(x) > −3, and every value above −3 is reached. The range is (−3, ∞).
The number of x-intercepts of the graph of y = 3^x + 2 is
3^x > 0, so 3^x + 2 > 2 for all x and the graph never meets the x-axis. Solving 3^x = −2 has no real solution.
The y-intercept of the graph of y = 5 − 2^x is
At x = 0, y = 5 − 2⁰ = 5 − 1 = 4. Forgetting that 2⁰ = 1 gives the tempting (0, 5).
Which of the following functions is strictly decreasing?
2^(−x) = (1/2)^x has base between 0 and 1, so it decreases. A base greater than 1, as in (3/2)^x, gives an increasing function.
The graph of y = a × b^x, where b > 0, passes through (0, 5) and (2, 20). The values of a and b are

−7π/6 is coterminal with 5π/6 (add 2π), which is in quadrant 2 with reference angle π/6. [1] sin(−7π/6) = 1/2 and cos(−7π/6) = −√3/2. [1]
A sector of a circle of radius 12 cm has area 54π cm². Find the angle at the centre in radians and the exact arc length of the sector. (2 marks)
Area = ½r²θ gives 54π = 72θ, so θ = 3π/4. [1] Arc length = rθ = 12 × 3π/4 = 9π cm. [1]
The exact value of sin(2π/3) + cos(5π/3) is:
sin(2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2 (second quadrant, sine positive). cos(5π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2 (fourth quadrant, cosine positive).
vce-methods12-graphs-of-sine-and-cosine: The function f(x) = 3 sin(2x) + 1 has amplitude and period
Amplitude = |3| = 3 (the +1 only shifts the graph up). Period = 2π/2 = π.
cos x ∈ [−1, 1], so −2cos x ∈ [−2, 2] and adding 4 gives [2, 6].
The period of y = cos(πx/2) is
A sine graph has maximum value 5, minimum value −1 and period 8. A possible rule is
Amplitude (5 − (−1))/2 = 3 and mean level (5 + (−1))/2 = 2. Period 8 = 2π/n gives n = π/4.
The number of x-intercepts of y = cos(2x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π is
cos(2x) = 0 when 2x = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 (2x ∈ [0, 4π]), so x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4: four intercepts.
For y = 2 sin(3x − π) + 1, state the amplitude, period, range and horizontal translation from y = 2 sin(3x) + 1, and find the y-intercept. (4 marks)
Write as 2 sin(3(x − π/3)) + 1; amplitude 2; period 2π/3; range [−1, 3]; translated π/3 to the right; y-intercept: 2 sin(−π) + 1 = 1.
Give the coordinates of the five key points of y = −cos(2x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ π, and describe the shape. (3 marks)
(0, −1), (π/4, 0), (π/2, 1), (3π/4, 0), (π, −1); one full period (period π), starting at a minimum, rising to a maximum at π/2 then returning; amplitude 1.

The depth of water in a harbour is h(t) = a cos(bt) + c metres, t hours after high tide at t = 0. High tide is 6 m and the next low tide is 2 m, 6 hours later. Find a, b and c, then find the times in [0, 12] when the depth is at least 5 m. (4 marks)
The period of y = sin(x/3) is
Period = 2π ÷ (1/3) = 6π. 2π/3 comes from multiplying by 1/3 instead of dividing.
The amplitude of y = −4 sin(x) is
Amplitude is the absolute value of the coefficient, so it is 4; the negative sign only reflects the graph in the x-axis.
The smallest positive x-intercept of y = sin(2x) is
sin(2x) = 0 when 2x = π, so x = π/2. Using x = π forgets that the period has been halved.
The range of y = 3 sin(x) − 2 is
3 sin x ∈ [−3, 3], and subtracting 2 gives [−5, 1]. The range [−3, 3] ignores the vertical translation.
The maximum value of y = 5 cos(2x) + 3 is
The maximum is amplitude plus mean level: 5 + 3 = 8. The 2 inside the bracket changes the period, not the maximum.
The graph of y = sin(x − π/4) is obtained from y = sin(x) by a translation of
Replacing x with (x − π/4) moves the graph π/4 units in the positive x direction, to the right. Left is the common mistake.
The smallest positive value of x for which y = cos(x + π/3) has a maximum is
cos(x + π/3) = 1 when x + π/3 = 2π, so x = 5π/3. Setting x + π/3 = 0 gives x = −π/3, which is negative.
The graph of y = sin(x) can be transformed onto y = cos(x) by translating it
cos(x) = sin(x + π/2), which is a translation of π/2 to the left. Translating right gives −cos(x).
The period of y = 2 sin(4πx) is
Period = 2π ÷ 4π = 1/2. The amplitude 2 does not affect the period.
The number of complete cycles of y = sin(3x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π is
The period is 2π/3, so 2π ÷ (2π/3) = 3 cycles fit in the interval. Six comes from wrongly multiplying the period by 2 instead of dividing.
The graph of y = sin(2x) is obtained from y = sin(x) by a dilation of
Replacing x with 2x compresses the graph horizontally, halving the period, so it is a dilation of factor 1/2 from the y-axis. A factor of 2 would stretch it.
A cosine graph has amplitude 2, period π and a maximum at (0, 2). A possible rule is
Period π gives n = 2π/π = 2, and a cosine graph starts at its maximum. y = 2cos(πx) has period 2, and sin(2x) would start at 0.
The number of solutions of sin(x) = 0.3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4π is
In each period of 2π the line y = 0.3 cuts the sine curve twice, so there are 4 solutions in two periods. Two solutions counts only one period.
Which statement about the graphs of sine and cosine is correct?
sin(−x) = −sin(x), so y = sin(x) has rotational symmetry about the origin
y = sin(x) is symmetric about the y-axis
y = cos(x) has rotational symmetry about the origin
sin is an odd function, so sin(−x) = −sin(x) and its graph has point symmetry about the origin. cos is even, so cos(−x) = cos(x) and its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
The first positive value of x at which y = 4 sin(x/2) reaches its maximum is
sin(x/2) = 1 when x/2 = π/2, so x = π. The period is 4π, so 4π is where it returns to zero after a full cycle, not the maximum.
Which of the following functions has period 2?
Period = 2π/π = 2 for y = sin(πx). sin(2πx) has period 1, sin(2x) has period π and sin(x/2) has period 4π.
Give the coordinates of the five key points of y = 3 sin(x/2) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4π. (3 marks)
Period = 2π ÷ (1/2) = 4π, so one full cycle is drawn [1]; amplitude 3 gives maximum 3 and minimum −3 [1]; key points (0, 0), (π, 3), (2π, 0), (3π, −3), (4π, 0) [1].
A cosine graph has a maximum value of 7, a minimum value of 1, period 4π and a maximum at x = 0. Find its rule in the form y = a cos(bx) + c. (3 marks)

The temperature T °C in a cool room is modelled by T = 15 − 6cos(πt/12), where t is the time in hours after midnight, 0 ≤ t ≤ 24. State the period, the maximum and minimum temperatures with the times they occur, and the temperature at 6 am. (4 marks)
Period = 2π ÷ (π/12) = 24 hours [1]; minimum 15 − 6 = 9 °C at t = 0 and t = 24 (midnight) [1]; maximum 15 + 6 = 21 °C at t = 12 (noon) [1]; at t = 6, cos(π/2) = 0 so T = 15 °C [1].
Describe the sequence of transformations that maps y = sin(x) onto y = −2 sin(x/3), and state the period and range of the image. (4 marks)
Dilation of factor 2 from the x-axis [1] and reflection in the x-axis [1]; dilation of factor 3 from the y-axis [1]; period 6π and range [−2, 2] [1].
For y = cos(2x + π/3) − 2, write the rule in the form y = cos(2(x − h)) + k, then state the translation from y = cos(2x), the period and the range. (4 marks)
y = cos(2(x + π/6)) − 2, so h = −π/6, k = −2 [1]; translated π/6 units to the left and 2 units down [1]; period 2π/2 = π [1]; range [−3, −1] [1].
A sine graph y = a sin(bx), with a > 0, has amplitude 3 and period 2π/3. Find a and b, then find the value of y when x = π/12. (3 marks)
For y = 2cos(x − π/3) with 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, find the coordinates of the maximum point and minimum point, and the y-intercept. (3 marks)
Maximum when x − π/3 = 0: (π/3, 2) [1]; minimum when x − π/3 = π: (4π/3, −2) [1]; y-intercept: 2cos(−π/3) = 1, so (0, 1) [1].
State the range of y = 4 − 3 sin(2x). (1 mark)
sin(2x) ∈ [−1, 1], so −3 sin(2x) ∈ [−3, 3] and the range is [1, 7] [1].
The function y = −3cos(πx/4) has amplitude and period
The amplitude is |−3| = 3 and the period is 2π ÷ (π/4) = 8. An amplitude cannot be negative, and 4 or π/4 results from misusing the formula for the period.
The range of y = 1 − 4 sin(x) is
sin(x) lies in [−1, 1], so −4 sin(x) lies in [−4, 4] and adding 1 gives [−3, 5]. The range [−4, 4] forgets the vertical translation.
A sine graph passes through (0, 1) rising, has maximum value 4, minimum value −2 and period π. A possible rule is
The centre is (4 + (−2))/2 = 1, the amplitude is 3 and b = 2π/π = 2, giving 3 sin(2x) + 1. Using 6 gives the full height of the graph rather than the amplitude.

The height H metres of a seat on a Ferris wheel is H(t) = 12 − 10cos(πt/20), where t is the time in seconds after the seat is at its lowest point. Find the period, the maximum height, the minimum height and the height at t = 10. (4 marks)
Period = 2π ÷ (π/20) = 40 seconds. [1] Maximum height = 12 + 10 = 22 m. [1] Minimum height = 12 − 10 = 2 m. [1] H(10) = 12 − 10cos(π/2) = 12 m. [1]
A function of the form y = a sin(bx), with a > 0 and b > 0, has period π and passes through the point (π/6, 2). Find the exact values of a and b. (3 marks)
Period π gives b = 2π/π = 2. [1] Substituting, a sin(π/3) = 2, so a(√3/2) = 2. [1] a = 4/√3 = 4√3/3. [1]
For y = 3sin(2x) + 1, the amplitude, period and range are:
Amplitude 3; period 2π/2 = π; the graph oscillates 3 units either side of y = 1.

The period of y = tan(2x) is
2π
π
The period of tan(nx) is π/n, so for n = 2 it is π/2.
methods12a2-tan-2
The vertical asymptotes of y = tan(x/2) for −2π < x < 2π are
x = ±π
Asymptotes occur when x/2 = π/2 + kπ, i.e. x = π + 2kπ. In (−2π, 2π) these are x = ±π.
methods12a2-tan-3
The x-intercepts of y = tan(x − π/4) are at
x = kπ
x = π/4 + kπ
x = −π/4 + kπ
x = 3π/4 + 2kπ
tan(x − π/4) = 0 when x − π/4 = kπ, so x = π/4 + kπ.
methods12a2-tan-4
The number of vertical asymptotes of y = tan(3x) in the interval (0, π) is
Asymptotes at 3x = π/2 + kπ, i.e. x = π/6, π/2, 5π/6 inside (0, π): three.
methods12a2-tan-5
The solutions of tan x = √3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π are
π/3 and 2π/3
π/3 and 4π/3
π/3 and 5π/3
π/6 and 7π/6
tan x = √3 gives reference angle π/3, and tan is positive in quadrants 1 and 3: x = π/3 and π + π/3 = 4π/3.
methods12a2-tan-6
Let f(x) = tan(2x − π/2) for 0 ≤ x ≤ π. State the period, the equations of the asymptotes and the x-intercepts. (4 marks)
Period π/2; asymptotes where 2x − π/2 = π/2 + kπ, i.e. x = π/2 + kπ/2, so x = 0, π/2, π; x-intercepts where 2x − π/2 = kπ, i.e. x = π/4 + kπ/2, so x = π/4 and 3π/4.
methods12a2-tan-7
Solve tan(2x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π. (3 marks)
2x ∈ [0, 2π]; tan = 1 at π/4 and π/4 + π = 5π/4; so 2x = π/4 or 5π/4; x = π/8 or 5π/8.
methods12a2-tan-8
Using the unit circle, explain why y = tan x has a vertical asymptote at x = π/2. (3 marks)

tan x = sin x / cos x, where the point on the unit circle is (cos x, sin x); at x = π/2 the point is (0, 1) so cos x = 0 and the quotient is undefined; as x approaches π/2 from below cos x → 0⁺ and tan x → +∞, from above cos x → 0⁻ and tan x → −∞, so the graph has a vertical asymptote.
methods12a2-tan-9
The period of y = tan(x/3) is
3π
6π
π
The period of tan(nx) is π/n, so for n = 1/3 it is π ÷ (1/3) = 3π. Choosing π/3 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
methods12a2-tan-10
The range of y = tan x is
all real numbers
On each branch tan x takes every real value, from −∞ to +∞. The restriction −1 ≤ y ≤ 1 belongs to sine and cosine, not tangent.
methods12a2-tan-11
The exact value of tan(5π/6) is
The reference angle is π/6 with tan = 1/√3, and tan is negative in the second quadrant. Giving +1/√3 ignores the quadrant sign.
methods12a2-tan-12
The exact value of tan(−π/3) is
tan is an odd function, so tan(−π/3) = −tan(π/3) = −√3. The value √3 forgets the negative sign.
methods12a2-tan-13
Which statement about y = tan x is correct?
It is an even function, symmetric about the y-axis
It is an odd function, with rotational symmetry about the origin
It is both even and odd
It is neither even nor odd
tan(−x) = sin(−x)/cos(−x) = −sin x/cos x = −tan x, so tan is odd. Cosine is the even function, which is where the first option comes from.
methods12a2-tan-14
The vertical asymptotes of y = tan(x + π/3) are at
x = π/6 + kπ
x = π/3 + kπ
x = −π/3 + kπ
x = 5π/6 + 2kπ
Set x + π/3 = π/2 + kπ, giving x = π/6 + kπ. The translation moves the asymptotes π/3 to the left, not to π/3 + kπ.
methods12a2-tan-15
Compared with the graph of y = tan x, the graph of y = 3 tan x has
period 3π and the same asymptotes
period π/3 and different asymptotes
period π and the same asymptotes, but steeper branches
period π and asymptotes at x = π/6 + kπ/3
A factor of 3 in front dilates the graph from the x-axis only, so the period and asymptotes are unchanged while the branches become steeper. Only a change inside the argument alters the period.
methods12a2-tan-16
If sin x = 3/5 and π/2 < x < π, then tan x equals
In the second quadrant cos x = −4/5, so tan x = (3/5) ÷ (−4/5) = −3/4. The value 3/4 ignores the negative cosine.
methods12a2-tan-17
The period of y = tan(πx) is
π
π²
The period of tan(nx) is π/n, so with n = π it is π/π = 1. Stating π ignores the coefficient of x.
methods12a2-tan-18
On the interval −π/2 < x < π/2, the graph of y = −tan x is
decreasing and passes through the origin
increasing and passes through the origin
decreasing with a y-intercept of −1
increasing with an asymptote at x = 0
The negative sign reflects y = tan x in the x-axis, so the increasing branch becomes decreasing, still through (0, 0). The asymptotes remain at x = ±π/2.
methods12a2-tan-19
The number of x-intercepts of y = tan(2x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ π is
tan(2x) = 0 when 2x = 0, π, 2π, so x = 0, π/2, π, which is three intercepts. Counting only the interior points gives 1, and forgetting the endpoint x = π gives 2.
methods12a2-tan-20
The period of y = 2 tan(3x) + 1 is
π
3π
Only the coefficient of x changes the period: π/3. The factor 2 and the shift +1 affect the dilation from the x-axis and the vertical position, not the period.
methods12a2-tan-21
A tangent graph passes through the origin and has consecutive asymptotes at x = −π/6 and x = π/6. Its equation is
y = tan(x/3)
y = tan(3x)
y = tan(6x)
y = tan(3x/2)
The asymptotes are π/3 apart, so the period is π/3 and n = π ÷ (π/3) = 3. Check: 3x = π/2 gives x = π/6. The equation y = tan(6x) would have period π/6.
methods12a2-tan-22
The value of tan(3π/2) is
undefined
At x = 3π/2, cos x = 0, so tan x = sin x / cos x is undefined; this is a vertical asymptote. The value 0 would need sin x = 0, but sin(3π/2) = −1.
methods12a2-tan-23
The domain of y = tan x is
all real x except x = π/2 + kπ, k ∈ Z
all real x except x = kπ, k ∈ Z
all real x except x = π/2 + 2kπ, k ∈ Z
tan x is undefined wherever cos x = 0, which is at every odd multiple of π/2. Excluding only x = kπ confuses the asymptotes with the x-intercepts.
methods12a2-tan-24
The solutions of tan x = 1/√3 for −π ≤ x ≤ π are
π/6 and 5π/6
−π/6 and 5π/6
π/6 and −5π/6
−π/6 and −5π/6
The principal solution is π/6, and subtracting the period π gives π/6 − π = −5π/6. The value 5π/6 has tan = −1/√3, so it is not a solution.
methods12a2-tan-25
The y-intercept of y = tan(x/2 + π/4) + 1 is
At x = 0, y = tan(π/4) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. Giving 1 forgets the vertical translation.
methods12a2-tan-26
State the period of y = 3 tan(4x) and find its vertical asymptotes for 0 ≤ x ≤ π/2. (3 marks)
Period = π/4 [1]. Asymptotes where 4x = π/2 + kπ, so x = π/8 + kπ/4 [1]. In the interval these are x = π/8 and x = 3π/8 [1].
methods12a2-tan-27
Solve tan x = −√3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. (2 marks)
Reference angle is π/3, and tan is negative in quadrants 2 and 4 [1]. x = π − π/3 = 2π/3 and x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3 [1].
methods12a2-tan-28
Solve tan(x − π/6) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. (3 marks)
Let u = x − π/6, so −π/6 ≤ u ≤ 11π/6 [1]. tan u = 1 gives u = π/4 or u = 5π/4 [1]. x = u + π/6, so x = 5π/12 or x = 17π/12 [1].
methods12a2-tan-29
Using sin(−x) = −sin x and cos(−x) = cos x, show that tan(−x) = −tan x. (2 marks)
tan(−x) = sin(−x) / cos(−x) [1] = −sin x / cos x = −tan x, so tan is an odd function [1].
methods12a2-tan-30
Let f(x) = tan(x + π/4) for −π ≤ x ≤ π. State the period, the equations of the asymptotes, the x-intercepts and the y-intercept. (4 marks)

Period π [1]. Asymptotes where x + π/4 = π/2 + kπ, so x = π/4 + kπ: x = −3π/4 and x = π/4 [1]. x-intercepts where x + π/4 = kπ, so x = −π/4 + kπ: x = −π/4 and x = 3π/4 [1]. y-intercept f(0) = tan(π/4) = 1 [1].
methods12a2-tan-31
A function of the form y = a tan(bx), where a and b are positive, has period π/2 and passes through the point (π/8, 3). Find a and b. (3 marks)
Period π/b = π/2, so b = 2 [1]. Substitute: 3 = a tan(2 × π/8) = a tan(π/4) = a [1]. So a = 3 and b = 2 [1].
methods12a2-tan-32
If sin x = −5/13 and π < x < 3π/2, find the exact value of tan x. (2 marks)
In the third quadrant cos x is negative, so cos x = −√(1 − 25/169) = −12/13 [1]. tan x = sin x / cos x = (−5/13) ÷ (−12/13) = 5/12 [1].
methods12a2-tan-33
Explain, using the unit circle, why the period of y = tan x is π. (3 marks)

tan x = sin x / cos x, where (cos x, sin x) is the point on the unit circle at angle x [1]. Adding π moves to the diametrically opposite point (−cos x, −sin x), so sine and cosine both change sign [1]. The ratio is unchanged, so tan(x + π) = tan x, and π is the smallest such shift [1].
methods12a2-tan-34
Solve tan(3x) = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π. (3 marks)
methods12a2-tan-35
Solve √3 tan x + 1 = 0 for −π ≤ x ≤ π. (3 marks)
tan x = −1/√3 [1]. Reference angle π/6, with tan negative in quadrants 2 and 4 [1]. x = 5π/6 and x = −π/6 [1].
methods12a2-tan-36
Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of y = tan x onto the graph of y = 2 tan(x/3) − 1, and state the period of the new graph. (4 marks)
Dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis [1]. Dilation by factor 3 from the y-axis [1]. Translation 1 unit down [1]. Period = π ÷ (1/3) = 3π [1].
methods12a2-tan-37
The value of y = −2 tan(x) at x = 3π/4 is
tan(3π/4) = −1, so y = −2 × (−1) = 2. Giving −2 ignores the negative sign of tan(3π/4).
methods12a2-tan-38
Solve tan(x) = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, giving answers correct to two decimal places. (2 marks)
The calculator gives the reference solution x = tan⁻¹(2) ≈ 1.11. [1] Tangent has period π, so the second solution is x = 1.11 + π ≈ 4.25. [1]
vce-methods12-tf-c1
The graph of y = tan(2x) has period and asymptotes:
Period 2π; asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ
Period π/2; asymptotes at x = π/4 + kπ/2
Period π; asymptotes at x = π/4 + kπ
Period π/2; asymptotes at x = kπ/2
tan has period π, so tan(2x) has period π/2. Asymptotes occur where 2x = π/2 + kπ, so x = π/4 + kπ/2, for integer k.
vce-methods12-solving-trigonometric-equa: The solutions of 2 sin x = √3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π are
sin x = √3/2 gives reference angle π/3; sin is positive in quadrants 1 and 2: x = π/3 and π − π/3 = 2π/3.
The solutions of cos(2x) = −1/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π are
2x ∈ [0, 2π]; cos θ = −1/2 at θ = 2π/3 and 4π/3. Halving: x = π/3 and 2π/3.
The number of solutions of 2 sin(3x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π is
sin(3x) = 1/2 with 3x ∈ [0, 6π]. Each 2π of 3x gives 2 solutions, so 3 × 2 = 6.
The solutions of tan x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π are
Reference angle π/4; tan is negative in quadrants 2 and 4: x = π − π/4 = 3π/4 and 2π − π/4 = 7π/4.
The complete solution set of 2cos²x − cos x = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π is
Factorise: cos x (2cos x − 1) = 0. cos x = 0 gives π/2, 3π/2; cos x = 1/2 gives π/3, 5π/3. Dividing by cos x would lose the first pair.
Solve 2sin²x + sin x − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. (4 marks)
Factorise: (2 sin x − 1)(sin x + 1) = 0; sin x = 1/2 gives x = π/6, 5π/6; sin x = −1 gives x = 3π/2; solutions x = π/6, 5π/6, 3π/2.
Solve √2 cos(2x − π/3) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π. (4 marks)
cos(2x − π/3) = 1/√2 = √2/2; let θ = 2x − π/3 ∈ [−π/3, 5π/3]; θ = −π/4 or π/4 (7π/4 is outside the interval); x = (θ + π/3)/2, so x = π/24 or x = 7π/24.
The temperature in a greenhouse is T(t) = 20 − 6cos(πt/12) °C, where t is hours after midnight, 0 ≤ t ≤ 24. Find when T = 23 and for how many hours T exceeds 23 °C. (4 marks)
T = 23: −6cos(πt/12) = 3, cos(πt/12) = −1/2; πt/12 = 2π/3 or 4π/3 so t = 8 or t = 16; T > 23 when cos is less than −1/2, i.e. 8 < t < 16: for 8 hours.
The solutions of sin x = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π are
The reference angle is π/6 and sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2, giving π/6 and π − π/6 = 5π/6. 7π/6 is in quadrant 3, where sine is negative.
The solutions of cos x = √2/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π are
Cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4, so x = π/4 and 2π − π/4 = 7π/4. 3π/4 is tempting but cosine is negative there.
The solutions of cos x = −1 for −2π ≤ x ≤ 2π are
cos x = −1 occurs at odd multiples of π, so x = −π and π in this interval. −2π, 0 and 2π are where cos x = 1.
The solutions of sin(2x) = √3/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π are
2x ∈ [0, 2π] and sin θ = √3/2 at θ = π/3 and 2π/3. Halving gives x = π/6 and π/3; forgetting to halve gives π/3 and 2π/3.
The solutions of tan(2x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π are
2x ∈ [0, 2π] and tan θ = 1 at θ = π/4 and 5π/4, so x = π/8 and 5π/8. 9π/8 lies outside the domain.
The solutions of 2cos(x/2) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4π are

A and B are mutually exclusive

A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue counters. Two counters are drawn with replacement. What is the probability that both are blue?
With replacement the draws are independent, so Pr(both blue) = 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36. The value 1/3 (6/10 × 5/9) is the answer if the counters are not replaced.

Given that Pr(A | B) = 0.35, what is Pr(A′ | B)?
Conditional probabilities given the same event B sum to 1 over A and A′, so Pr(A′ | B) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

In a population, 5% of people have a condition. A test is positive for 90% of people with the condition and for 10% of people without it. What is the probability that a randomly chosen person tests positive?
Pr(positive) = 0.05 × 0.9 + 0.95 × 0.1 = 0.045 + 0.095 = 0.14. The value 0.045 counts only those who have the condition.
methods12a3-cp-27
A and B are independent with Pr(A) = 0.4 and Pr(B) = 0.3. What is Pr(A | B′)?
A and B′ are independent, so Pr(A | B′) = Pr(A) = 0.4. The value 0.28 is Pr(A ∩ B′), not the conditional probability.

(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen Physics student is a girl. (c) Are 'being a girl' and 'studying Physics' independent? Justify. (4 marks)
(a) 30/70 = 3/7 [1] (b) 30/45 = 2/3 [1] (c) Pr(Physics) = 45/120 = 3/8 [1] Pr(Physics | girl) = 3/7 ≠ 3/8, so the events are not independent [1]

methods12a3-cp-38
Pr(A ∩ B′) = 0.2 and Pr(B′) = 0.5. What is Pr(A | B′)?
Pr(A | B′) = Pr(A ∩ B′) ÷ Pr(B′) = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4. Using 0.1, the product, is multiplying instead of dividing.

How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word BANANA?
There are 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N repeated 2 times: 6!/(3! × 2!) = 720/12 = 60. 720 ignores the repeats.

A committee of 3 people is chosen from 8 people. How many different committees are possible?
Order does not matter, so ⁸C₃ = 8!/(3! × 5!) = 56. 336 = ⁸P₃ counts ordered selections.
methods12a3-pc-3
Four different books are chosen from 7 and placed in order on a shelf. How many arrangements are possible?
Order matters and no book is reused: ⁷P₄ = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. 35 is ⁷C₄ and 2401 would be 7⁴.
methods12a3-pc-4
How many 4-digit PINs can be made from the digits 0 to 9 if digits may be repeated but the first digit cannot be 0?
First digit: 9 choices; each of the other three digits: 10 choices. 9 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 9000. 4536 would be the answer if repeats were not allowed.
