Given that ⁿC₂ = 45, the value of n is
n(n − 1)/2 = 45 gives n(n − 1) = 90, so n = 10 (⁹C₂ = 36 and ¹¹C₂ = 55).
methods12a3-pc-6
Five people, including Alice and Ben, sit in a row of five chairs. (a) How many arrangements have Alice and Ben sitting next to each other? (b) How many have them not next to each other? (3 marks)
(a) Treat Alice and Ben as one block: 4! arrangements of 4 objects × 2! orders within the block = 48 (2 marks); (b) total 5! = 120, so 120 − 48 = 72 (1 mark).
methods12a3-pc-7
A team of 4 is chosen from 6 boys and 5 girls. How many teams contain at least 2 girls? (3 marks)

Cases: 2 girls, 2 boys = ⁵C₂ × ⁶C₂ = 10 × 15 = 150; 3 girls, 1 boy = ⁵C₃ × ⁶C₁ = 10 × 6 = 60; 4 girls = ⁵C₄ = 5 (2 marks for correct cases). Total = 150 + 60 + 5 = 215 (1 mark). Check: ¹¹C₄ = 330, minus 0 girls (15) and 1 girl (100) = 215.
methods12a3-pc-8
How many even 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 if no digit is used more than once? (3 marks)
The last digit must be even: 3 choices (2, 4 or 6) (1 mark); the other three places are filled from the remaining 5 digits in order: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 (1 mark); total 3 × 60 = 180 (1 mark).
methods12a3-pc-9
The value of 7!/5! is
7!/5! = 7 × 6 = 42, since the 5! cancels. 35 would come from 7 × 5.
methods12a3-pc-10
The value of ¹⁰C₈ is
¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = 10 × 9/2 = 45. 90 is ¹⁰P₂, which counts ordered selections.
methods12a3-pc-11
How many different arrangements are there of the four letters of the word MATH?
All four letters are different, so there are 4! = 24 arrangements. 16 would be 4² and wrongly allows letters to be reused.
methods12a3-pc-12
Eight runners compete in a race. In how many ways can first, second and third places be filled?
Order matters, so ⁸P₃ = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. 56 is ⁸C₃, which ignores who finishes in which place.
methods12a3-pc-13
The value of ⁵P₂ is
⁵P₂ = 5 × 4 = 20. 10 is ⁵C₂, which divides by 2! because it ignores order.
methods12a3-pc-14
How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word TOOTH?
There are 5 letters with T repeated twice and O repeated twice: 5!/(2! × 2!) = 120/4 = 30. 60 only divides out one of the repeated pairs.
methods12a3-pc-15
If ⁿP₂ = 56, then n equals
n(n − 1) = 56 gives n = 8, since 8 × 7 = 56. n = 7 gives only 42.
methods12a3-pc-16
An outfit consists of one of 4 shirts, one of 3 pairs of trousers and one of 2 hats. How many different outfits are possible?
By the multiplication principle, 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Adding the numbers (4 + 3 + 2 = 9) is a common mistake.
methods12a3-pc-17
Given that ⁹C₂ = ⁹Cₖ and k ≠ 2, the value of k is
Using ⁿCᵣ = ⁿC₍ₙ₋ᵣ₎, ⁹C₂ = ⁹C₇. A value of 6 does not work, since ⁹C₆ = 84 but ⁹C₂ = 36.
methods12a3-pc-18
At a meeting, each of 12 people shakes hands exactly once with every other person. How many handshakes occur?
Each handshake is an unordered pair, so ¹²C₂ = 66. 132 is ¹²P₂, which counts each handshake twice.
methods12a3-pc-19
How many 3-letter codes can be made from the letters A, B, C, D, E if letters may be repeated?
Each of the three positions has 5 choices, so 5³ = 125. 60 is the answer if repeats were not allowed.
methods12a3-pc-20
Three boys and three girls sit in a row so that boys and girls alternate. How many arrangements are possible?
Either a boy or a girl can start (2 ways), then the boys can be ordered 3! ways and the girls 3! ways: 2 × 6 × 6 = 72. 36 forgets that the pattern can start with either sex.
methods12a3-pc-21
How many diagonals does a hexagon have?
Choose any 2 of the 6 vertices: ⁶C₂ = 15, then subtract the 6 sides to leave 9 diagonals. 15 counts the sides as well.
methods12a3-pc-22
A group of 5 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women so that it has exactly 3 men and 2 women. How many different groups are possible?
Choose the men and women separately: ⁵C₃ × ⁴C₂ = 10 × 6 = 60. 126 is ⁹C₅, which ignores the restriction on numbers of men and women.
methods12a3-pc-23
How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1 to 9 if no digit is repeated?
Order matters and digits are not reused: ⁹P₄ = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3024. 6561 = 9⁴ allows repeats, and 126 is ⁹C₄.
methods12a3-pc-24
How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word MISSISSIPPI?
There are 11 letters with I repeated 4 times, S 4 times and P twice: 11!/(4! × 4! × 2!) = 39 916 800/1152 = 34 650.
methods12a3-pc-25
A committee of 4 is chosen from 9 people. How many committees include one particular person, Sam?
Sam is already in, so choose the other 3 from the remaining 8: ⁸C₃ = 56. 126 is the number of committees with no condition on Sam.
methods12a3-pc-26
How many odd 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit is repeated?
The last digit is odd (1, 3 or 5): 3 choices. The first two digits are then filled in 4 × 3 ways, giving 3 × 12 = 36. 60 counts all 3-digit numbers, odd or even.
methods12a3-pc-27
Evaluate ⁷C₃ and ⁷P₃, showing your working. (2 marks)
methods12a3-pc-28
How many 4-digit numbers greater than 3000 can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if digits may be repeated? (2 marks)
The first digit must be 3, 4 or 5, so there are 3 choices [1]; each of the other three digits has 5 choices, so 3 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 375 [1].
methods12a3-pc-29
Solve ⁿP₂ = 12 for n, where n is a positive integer. (2 marks)
n(n − 1) = 12, so n² − n − 12 = 0, giving (n − 4)(n + 3) = 0 [1]; n must be positive, so n = 4 [1].
methods12a3-pc-30
A committee of 5 is chosen from 7 men and 5 women. (a) How many committees are possible with no restrictions? (b) How many contain exactly 3 women? (c) How many contain at least one man? (4 marks)
(a) ¹²C₅ = 792 [1]; (b) ⁵C₃ × ⁷C₂ = 10 × 21 = 210 [1] [1]; (c) subtract the all-women committees: 792 − ⁵C₅ = 792 − 1 = 791 [1].
methods12a3-pc-31
Evaluate ⁸C₃ + ⁸C₄ and show that it equals ⁹C₄. (3 marks)
⁸C₃ = 56 [1]; ⁸C₄ = 70, so the sum is 126 [1]; ⁹C₄ = (9 × 8 × 7 × 6)/24 = 126, so the two are equal [1].
methods12a3-pc-32
Eight runners compete in a race with gold, silver and bronze medals awarded to the first three. In how many ways can the medals be awarded if runner A must win a medal? (3 marks)
Runner A can take any one of the 3 medals: 3 ways [1]; the other two medals go to 2 of the remaining 7 runners in order: ⁷P₂ = 42 ways [1]; total 3 × 42 = 126 [1].
methods12a3-pc-33
(a) How many 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 0 to 9 if no digit is repeated and the first digit is not 0? (b) How many of these numbers are divisible by 5? (4 marks)

(a) 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4536 [1]; (b) ends in 0: 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 [1]; ends in 5: first digit has 8 choices (not 0 or 5), then 8 × 7 for the middle digits, giving 8 × 8 × 7 = 448 [1]; total 504 + 448 = 952 [1].
methods12a3-pc-34
A pizza shop offers 6 different toppings. A customer chooses either 2 or 3 different toppings. How many different choices of toppings are possible? (2 marks)
Choosing 2 toppings: ⁶C₂ = 15, and choosing 3 toppings: ⁶C₃ = 20 [1]; the cases are exclusive, so total 15 + 20 = 35 [1].
methods12a3-pc-35
Three couples sit in a row of six chairs so that each couple sits together. How many seating arrangements are possible? (3 marks)
Treat each couple as a block; the 3 blocks can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways [1]; within each block the two people can swap, giving 2³ = 8 ways [1]; total 6 × 8 = 48 [1].
methods12a3-pc-36
A hand of 5 cards is dealt from a standard pack of 52 cards, which contains 13 hearts. How many hands contain exactly 2 hearts? (3 marks)
Choose the 2 hearts from 13: ¹³C₂ = 78 [1]; choose the other 3 cards from the 39 non-hearts: ³⁹C₃ = 9139 [1]; total 78 × 9139 = 712 842 [1].
methods12a3-pc-37
How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word LETTER?
There are 6 letters with T repeated twice and E repeated twice, so 6!/(2! × 2!) = 720/4 = 180. Dividing by only one factorial of 2 gives 360.
methods12a3-pc-38
Seven people stand in a line. In how many ways can they stand if Chen must not be at either end? (2 marks)
Chen can take any of the 5 middle positions. [1] The other 6 people can be arranged in 6! = 720 ways, so the total is 5 × 720 = 3600. [1]
vce-methods12-pc-c1
A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. How many committees include at least one girl?
Total ⁹C₃ = 84; all-boy committees ⁵C₃ = 10. 84 − 10 = 74. Counting cases directly also works: 4 × 10 + 6 × 5 + 4 = 74.
vce-methods12-rates-of-change: The average rate of change of f(x) = x² from x = 1 to x = 4 is
(f(4) − f(1))/(4 − 1) = (16 − 1)/3 = 5. 15 is the change in f without dividing by the change in x.
A particle's displacement is s(t) = 3t² + 2t metres, t in seconds. Its average velocity from t = 0 to t = 2 is
s(2) = 12 + 4 = 16 and s(0) = 0, so the average velocity is 16/2 = 8 m s⁻¹. 16 is the displacement; 14 would be the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.
The volume V (in litres) of water in a tank is modelled over time t (in minutes). The average rate of change of V with respect to t has units
Average rate of change = change in V divided by change in t, so the units are litres per minute.
The graph of the volume of water in a tank against time is a straight line from (0, 50) to (10, 20), with volume in litres and time in minutes. The rate of change of volume is
Gradient = (20 − 50)/(10 − 0) = −3 L min⁻¹. The negative sign shows the volume is decreasing.
For f(x) = x², the gradient of the secant through (1, f(1)) and (1 + h, f(1 + h)) is
((1 + h)² − 1)/h = (2h + h²)/h = 2 + h. As h → 0 this approaches 2, the gradient of the tangent.
Let f(x) = x³ − 2x. (a) Find the average rate of change of f from x = 1 to x = 3. (b) What does this value represent geometrically? (3 marks)
(a) f(3) = 27 − 6 = 21 and f(1) = 1 − 2 = −1 (1 mark); average rate = (21 − (−1))/(3 − 1) = 22/2 = 11 (1 mark); (b) it is the gradient of the secant (chord) joining (1, −1) and (3, 21) (1 mark).

The number of bacteria in a culture after t hours is P(t) = 500 + 40t². (a) Find the average rate of change from t = 0 to t = 3. (b) Find the average rate of change from t = 3 to t = 4. (c) Comment on the difference. (3 marks)

(a) P(3) = 860, P(0) = 500, so (860 − 500)/3 = 120 bacteria per hour (1 mark); (b) P(4) = 1140, so (1140 − 860)/1 = 280 bacteria per hour (1 mark); (c) the growth rate is increasing over time, as expected for a quadratic with positive coefficient (1 mark).

A cup of tea cools. Its temperature is 90 °C at t = 0 minutes, 60 °C at t = 5 minutes and 45 °C at t = 10 minutes. Find the average rate of change of temperature over each 5-minute interval and interpret the two values. (3 marks)

0 to 5 min: (60 − 90)/5 = −6 °C per minute (1 mark); 5 to 10 min: (45 − 60)/5 = −3 °C per minute (1 mark); the tea is cooling in both intervals (negative rates) but the rate of cooling slows down as it approaches room temperature (1 mark).
The average rate of change of f(x) = x² − 3x from x = 2 to x = 5 is
f(5) = 10 and f(2) = −2, so the average rate is (10 − (−2))/(5 − 2) = 12/3 = 4. 12 is only the change in f, not divided by the change in x.
A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. Its average speed is
Average speed = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km h⁻¹. 75 comes from dividing by 2 instead of 2.5, and 375 from multiplying.
The instantaneous rate of change of f(x) = x² at x = 3 is
((3 + h)² − 9)/h = 6 + h, which approaches 6 as h → 0. 9 is the value f(3), not the rate of change.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function at x = a is best described as
the average rate of change over a very long interval
the limit of the average rate of change over [a, a + h] as h approaches 0
the change in y divided by the change in x between two fixed points
the value of the function at x = a
Shrinking the interval so that h → 0 turns the secant gradient into the tangent gradient. A fixed interval always gives an average rate, not an instantaneous one.
A particle has displacement s(t) = t² + 4t metres at time t seconds. Its instantaneous velocity at t = 3 is
s′(t) = 2t + 4, so s′(3) = 10 m s⁻¹. 7 m s⁻¹ is the average velocity from t = 0 to t = 3 (21/3), and 21 is the displacement at t = 3.
The gradient of the tangent to y = x³ at x = 2 is
dy/dx = 3x², so at x = 2 the gradient is 3 × 4 = 12. 8 is the y-value at x = 2, not the gradient.
The average rate of change of f(x) = x³ from x = 0 to x = 2 is
(f(2) − f(0))/(2 − 0) = (8 − 0)/2 = 4. 8 is the change in f without dividing by the change in x.
The average rate of change of f(x) = 5 − 2x over the interval [1, 10] is
f(10) = −15 and f(1) = 3, so the average rate is −18/9 = −2, the gradient of the line. −18 is the change in f only.
The height h(t) of a ball is changing at an instantaneous rate that is negative at t = 4. At that moment the ball's height is
A negative instantaneous rate of change means the quantity is decreasing. The rate being negative does not mean the height itself is zero or negative.
For f(x) = x³, the gradient of the secant through (1, f(1)) and (1 + h, f(1 + h)) is
((1 + h)³ − 1)/h = (3h + 3h² + h³)/h = 3 + 3h + h². The value 3 is only the limit as h → 0, not the secant gradient for a fixed h.
The average rate of change of a function f over the interval [2, 6] is 5, and f(2) = 7. The value of f(6) is
f(6) − f(2) = 5 × (6 − 2) = 20, so f(6) = 27. 32 comes from using 5 × 6 + 2, and 12 from adding 5 to f(2).
The volume of water in a tank is V(t) = 400 − 20t litres after t minutes. The rate of change of the volume is
V is linear with gradient −20, so the volume falls by 20 L every minute. 20 L min⁻¹ ignores the sign and so misses that the tank is draining.
A particle has displacement s(t) = t³ − 6t² metres at time t seconds. Its instantaneous velocity at t = 2 is
s′(t) = 3t² − 12t, so s′(2) = 12 − 24 = −12 m s⁻¹, meaning it moves in the negative direction. −16 is the displacement s(2), not the velocity.
A ball is thrown upwards and caught at the height it was launched from. Over the whole flight, its average velocity is
equal to half its launch speed
Average velocity is total displacement divided by time, and the displacement is zero because the ball returns to its start. Average speed, using distance, would not be zero.
For the linear function f(x) = mx + c, the average rate of change between any two values of x
depends on which two values are chosen
(m·b + c − m·a − c)/(b − a) = m for every interval, since the graph has constant gradient. c is the y-intercept and has no effect on the rate.
The average rate of change of f(x) = 1/x from x = 1 to x = 4 is
f(4) = 1/4 and f(1) = 1, so the rate is (1/4 − 1)/(4 − 1) = (−3/4)/3 = −1/4. 1/4 loses the negative sign, which shows f is decreasing.
Let f(x) = x² + 3x. Find the average rate of change of f from x = 1 to x = 5. (2 marks)

Let s(t) = t² metres be the displacement of a particle at time t seconds. (a) Find and simplify the gradient of the secant between t = 2 and t = 2 + h. (b) Hence find the instantaneous velocity at t = 2. (3 marks)
(a) s(2 + h) − s(2) = (4 + 4h + h²) − 4 = 4h + h² [1]; gradient = (4h + h²)/h = 4 + h [1]; (b) as h → 0, 4 + h → 4, so the instantaneous velocity is 4 m s⁻¹ [1].

A car's distance from its starting point is 0 km at t = 0 h, 50 km at t = 2 h and 140 km at t = 5 h. Find its average speed over (a) the first 2 hours, (b) the last 3 hours and (c) the whole trip. Explain why the answer to (c) is not the mean of the answers to (a) and (b). (3 marks)

(a) 50/2 = 25 km h⁻¹ and (b) (140 − 50)/3 = 30 km h⁻¹ [1]; (c) 140/5 = 28 km h⁻¹ [1]; the mean of 25 and 30 is 27.5, which differs because the two intervals have different lengths (2 h and 3 h), so the average must be weighted by time [1].

Let f(x) = x² − 4x. (a) Find the average rate of change of f from x = 1 to x = 3. (b) Use first principles to find the instantaneous rate of change of f at x = 3. (c) Find the value of x at which the instantaneous rate of change is zero. (4 marks)

(a) f(3) = −3 and f(1) = −3, so the average rate is 0/2 = 0 [1]; (b) f(3 + h) − f(3) = (9 + 6h + h² − 12 − 4h) − (−3) = 2h + h² [1]; dividing by h gives 2 + h, which approaches 2 as h → 0, so the instantaneous rate is 2 [1]; (c) f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2 [1].
The population of a town was 12 000 at the start of 2010 and 15 600 at the start of 2020. Find the average rate of change of the population per year over this period. (2 marks)
Change in population = 15 600 − 12 000 = 3600 over 10 years [1]; average rate = 3600/10 = 360 people per year [1].

A particle has displacement s(t) = 2t³ − t metres at time t seconds. (a) Find its average velocity from t = 1 to t = 3. (b) Find its instantaneous velocity at t = 2. (c) Explain why these two values differ. (4 marks)

(a) s(3) = 51 and s(1) = 1 [1]; average velocity = (51 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 25 m s⁻¹ [1]; (b) s′(t) = 6t² − 1, so s′(2) = 23 m s⁻¹ [1]; (c) the velocity is not constant, so the average over an interval need not equal the instantaneous value at its midpoint [1].
Explain the difference between the average rate of change and the instantaneous rate of change of the position of a car, and state how each is shown on a graph of position against time. (2 marks)

The average rate is the change in position divided by the change in time over an interval, shown as the gradient of a secant (chord) [1]; the instantaneous rate is the rate at a single moment, like a speedometer reading, found as the limit as the interval shrinks to zero and shown as the gradient of the tangent [1].

The cost of producing q items is C(q) = 500 + 4q² dollars. (a) Find the average rate of change of C from q = 10 to q = 20. (b) Find the instantaneous rate of change of C at q = 10, given that C′(q) = 8q. (3 marks)
A plant is 12 cm tall at week 2 and 30 cm tall at week 8. Find its average growth rate in cm per week. (1 mark)
Let f(x) = x² − 6x + 1. Find the value of x at which the instantaneous rate of change of f equals the average rate of change of f over the interval [0, 4]. (4 marks)
The average rate of change of f(x) = 2x² − x from x = 1 to x = 3 is
f(1) = 1 and f(3) = 15, so the average rate of change is (15 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 7. Giving 14 forgets to divide by the interval width.
Let f(x) = 3x² − 2x. (a) Find and simplify the gradient of the secant through (1, f(1)) and (1 + h, f(1 + h)). (b) Hence find the instantaneous rate of change of f at x = 1. (3 marks)
f(1) = 1 and f(1 + h) = 3(1 + h)² − 2(1 + h) = 1 + 4h + 3h². [1] Secant gradient = (4h + 3h²)/h = 4 + 3h. [1] As h → 0, the instantaneous rate of change at x = 1 is 4. [1]

The height of a rocket is h(t) = 40t − 5t² metres, t seconds after launch. (a) Find the average velocity from t = 0 to t = 2. (b) Find the average velocity from t = 2 to t = 4. (c) Explain what the difference between these values shows about the rocket. (3 marks)

(a) h(0) = 0 and h(2) = 60, so the average velocity is 60/2 = 30 m/s. [1] (b) h(4) = 80, so the average velocity is (80 − 60)/2 = 10 m/s. [1] (c) The average velocity is smaller later, so the rocket is slowing down. [1]
The average rate of change of f(x) = x² − 3x from x = 1 to x = 4 is:
(f(4) − f(1)) ÷ (4 − 1) = (4 − (−2)) ÷ 3 = 2. It is the gradient of the chord, not the derivative at a point.
vce-methods12-differentiation-from-first: Which expression defines the derivative f′(x) from first principles?
The derivative is the limit of the gradient of the secant, [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, as h → 0. Option B has the numerator reversed, giving −f′(x).
For f(x) = x², the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
((x + h)² − x²)/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. Letting h → 0 then gives f′(x) = 2x.
For f(x) = x³, the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
(x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, so the numerator is 3x²h + 3xh² + h³ and dividing by h gives 3x² + 3xh + h².
Using first principles, the gradient of the tangent to y = x² at x = 2 is found from lim (h→0) [(2 + h)² − 4]/h. This limit equals
((2 + h)² − 4)/h = (4h + h²)/h = 4 + h, which tends to 4 as h → 0.
Which of the following functions is not differentiable at x = 0?
The graph of |x| has a sharp corner at the origin: the gradient is −1 from the left and +1 from the right, so the limit defining f′(0) does not exist. The other functions are smooth polynomials.
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = x² + 3x. (3 marks)
[f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = [(x + h)² + 3(x + h) − x² − 3x]/h (1 mark) = (2xh + h² + 3h)/h = 2x + 3 + h (1 mark); as h → 0, f′(x) = 2x + 3 (1 mark).
Use first principles to find f′(3) for f(x) = 2x² − x. (3 marks)
Use first principles to show that the derivative of f(x) = x³ − x is f′(x) = 3x² − 1. (3 marks)
f(x + h) − f(x) = (x + h)³ − (x + h) − x³ + x = 3x²h + 3xh² + h³ − h (1 mark); dividing by h: 3x² + 3xh + h² − 1 (1 mark); as h → 0 this tends to 3x² − 1 (1 mark).
For f(x) = x, the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
(x + h − x)/h = h/h = 1, so f′(x) = 1 for every x. It does not depend on x because the graph is a straight line of gradient 1.
Using first principles, the derivative of the constant function f(x) = 5 is
f(x + h) − f(x) = 5 − 5 = 0, so the quotient is 0/h = 0 for every h ≠ 0, and the limit is 0. It is not undefined, because h is never actually zero in the quotient.
For f(x) = 3x², the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
3(x + h)² − 3x² = 6xh + 3h², and dividing by h gives 6x + 3h. Forgetting to multiply the h term by 3 gives 6x + h, which is wrong.
In the first-principles definition of the derivative, h represents
the horizontal distance between the two points on the secant
the vertical change in the function
h is the horizontal step from x to x + h. The vertical change is f(x + h) − f(x), which is the numerator of the quotient.
Using first principles, f′(−1) for f(x) = x² is found from lim (h→0) [(−1 + h)² − 1]/h. This limit equals
((−1 + h)² − 1)/h = (−2h + h²)/h = −2 + h, which tends to −2. Taking the limit as 2 comes from forgetting the sign of the −1.
Why can h = 0 not simply be substituted into [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h to find the derivative?
It gives 0/0, which is undefined, so the expression must first be simplified
It gives the function value f(x) itself
h = 0 is only allowed for linear functions
With h = 0 both numerator and denominator are zero, giving the undefined form 0/0. After the factor h is cancelled, the limit as h → 0 can be evaluated.
For f(x) = 2x², the gradient of the tangent at x = 3, found from first principles, is
[2(3 + h)² − 18]/h = (12h + 2h²)/h = 12 + 2h, which tends to 12. The value 18 is f(3), not the gradient.
the value of the function at x = 3
the area under y = x² near x = 3
the gradient of y = x² at x = 6
the gradient of the tangent to y = x² at x = 3, which is 6
The quotient is the secant gradient between x = 3 and x = 3 + h on y = x², and (6h + h²)/h = 6 + h → 6. It is the gradient at x = 3, not at x = 6.
The derivative of f(x) = x² − 4x, found from first principles, is f′(x) = 2x − 4. At which value of x is the tangent horizontal?
A horizontal tangent has gradient 0, so 2x − 4 = 0 and x = 2. The value x = 4 is where the function is zero, not where its gradient is zero.
A function has a jump discontinuity at x = a. Which statement is correct?
It is differentiable at x = a only if the jump is small
It is differentiable at x = a with f′(a) = 0
It is not differentiable at x = a
It is differentiable at x = a from the left only, so the derivative exists
A function must be continuous at a point to be differentiable there. At a jump the secant gradients become unbounded, so the limit does not exist.
Using first principles, the derivative of f(x) = 4x − 7 is
[4(x + h) − 7 − 4x + 7]/h = 4h/h = 4. The constant −7 disappears because it cancels in f(x + h) − f(x).
For f(x) = x³, the gradient of the tangent at x = 2 is found from lim (h→0) [(2 + h)³ − 8]/h. This limit equals
(2 + h)³ − 8 = 12h + 6h² + h³, so the quotient is 12 + 6h + h², which tends to 12. The value 8 is f(2), not the gradient.
For f(x) = ax², where a is a constant, the derivative from first principles is
[a(x + h)² − ax²]/h = (2axh + ah²)/h = 2ax + ah, which tends to 2ax as h → 0. The constant a stays as a factor.
The distance of a particle is s = t² metres after t seconds. Its instantaneous velocity at t = 1, from first principles, is the limit of [(1 + h)² − 1]/h as h → 0. This is
[(1 + h)² − 1]/h = 2 + h, which tends to 2 m/s. The expression 2 + h is the average velocity over a time interval of length h, not the instantaneous value.
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = 4x² + 5. (3 marks)
Use first principles to show that the derivative of f(x) = 1/x is f′(x) = −1/x². (4 marks)
[f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = [1/(x + h) − 1/x]/h [1]; combine over a common denominator: [x − (x + h)]/[x(x + h)] = −h/[x(x + h)] [1]; dividing by h gives −1/[x(x + h)] [1]; as h → 0, f′(x) = −1/x² [1].
Use first principles to find f′(−2) for f(x) = x² − 5x. (3 marks)
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = 2x³. (3 marks)
Show, using one-sided limits of the first-principles quotient, that f(x) = |x| is not differentiable at x = 0. (3 marks)

The quotient at x = 0 is [f(h) − f(0)]/h = |h|/h [1]; for h > 0 this equals 1, so the limit from the right is 1 [1]; for h < 0 it equals −1, so the limit from the left is −1; the two limits differ, so f′(0) does not exist [1].
Use first principles to find the gradient of y = x² − x at x = 2, and hence find the equation of the tangent at x = 2. (4 marks)
f(2) = 2 and f(2 + h) = 4 + 4h + h² − 2 − h = 2 + 3h + h² [1]; [f(2 + h) − f(2)]/h = 3 + h [1]; as h → 0 the gradient is 3 [1]; tangent: y − 2 = 3(x − 2), so y = 3x − 4 [1].
Use the first-principles derivative of f(x) = x² to find the coordinates of the point on y = x² where the tangent has gradient 6. (3 marks)
[(x + h)² − x²]/h = 2x + h [1]; as h → 0, f′(x) = 2x [1]; 2x = 6 gives x = 3, so the point is (3, 9) [1].
A student writes that the derivative of f(x) = x² is 2x + h. Explain the error and give the correct derivative. (2 marks)
2x + h is the gradient of the secant for a particular value of h; the derivative requires taking the limit as h → 0 [1]; this gives the correct derivative f′(x) = 2x [1].
For f(x) = x² + x, the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
f(x + h) − f(x) = 2xh + h² + h, and dividing by h gives 2x + h + 1. The expression 2x + 1 is the limit as h → 0, not the quotient.
The gradient of y = x³ at x = −1, found from lim (h→0) [(−1 + h)³ + 1]/h, is
(−1 + h)³ + 1 = 3h − 3h² + h³, so the quotient is 3 − 3h + h², which tends to 3. A negative answer comes from sign errors in the expansion.
For f(x) = 1/x, the expression [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplifies to
[1/(x + h) − 1/x]/h = [(x − (x + h))/(x(x + h))]/h = −1/(x(x + h)). The answer −1/x² is the limit as h → 0, not the quotient.
For f(x) = −x², first principles gives the derivative f′(x) =
The quotient is (−2xh − h²)/h = −2x − h, and as h → 0 the limit is −2x. Including h in the answer leaves a term that vanishes in the limit.
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = 3x² − 2x + 1. (3 marks)
Use first principles to show that the derivative of f(x) = x⁴ is f′(x) = 4x³. (4 marks)
(x + h)⁴ = x⁴ + 4x³h + 6x²h² + 4xh³ + h⁴. [1] f(x + h) − f(x) = 4x³h + 6x²h² + 4xh³ + h⁴. [1] Dividing by h gives 4x³ + 6x²h + 4xh² + h³. [1] As h → 0, f′(x) = 4x³. [1]
Use first principles to find the gradient of y = x² + 2x at x = −1, and hence the equation of the tangent at that point. (3 marks)
f(−1 + h) = (−1 + h)² + 2(−1 + h) = −1 + h², and f(−1) = −1, so the quotient is h²/h = h. [1] As h → 0 the gradient is 0. [1] The tangent passes through (−1, −1), so its equation is y = −1. [1]
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = x² + 3x.
[f(x + h) − f(x)] ÷ h = [(x + h)² + 3(x + h) − x² − 3x] ÷ h = (2xh + h² + 3h) ÷ h = 2x + h + 3. As h → 0, this approaches 2x + 3.
vce-methods12-derivatives-of-polynomials: Differentiate term by term: 12x² − 10x, and the derivative of the constant 7 is 0. Option A wrongly keeps the constant.
Let f(x) = (2x + 1)(x − 3). The value of f′(2) is
Expand: f(x) = 2x² − 5x − 3, so f′(x) = 4x − 5 and f′(2) = 8 − 5 = 3.
The gradient of the curve y = x³ − 3x is zero when
At which value of x is the gradient of y = x² − 4x equal to 6?
The derivative of f(x) = (x² + 1)² with respect to x is
Expand: f(x) = x⁴ + 2x² + 1, so f′(x) = 4x³ + 4x. Option A forgets the inner derivative 2x.
Let f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 4. Find f′(x) and the values of x for which f′(x) = 0. (3 marks)
f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 (1 mark); = 6(x − 1)(x − 2) (1 mark); so f′(x) = 0 when x = 1 or x = 2 (1 mark).
The curve y = x² + bx + c passes through (0, 3) and has gradient 2 at x = 1. Find b and c. (3 marks)
dy/dx = 2x + b (1 mark); at x = 1: 2 + b = 2, so b = 0 (1 mark); y(0) = c = 3 (1 mark). The curve is y = x² + 3.
The height of a ball above the ground is h(t) = 20t − 5t² metres, t seconds after it is thrown upward. (a) Find h′(t). (b) Find when the velocity is zero and the height at that time. (3 marks)
(a) h′(t) = 20 − 10t (1 mark); (b) 20 − 10t = 0 gives t = 2 s (1 mark); h(2) = 40 − 20 = 20 m, the maximum height (1 mark).
Find the gradient of the curve y = x³ − 4x² + x at x = 3. (2 marks)
Find the equation of the tangent to y = x² − 3x + 2 at the point where x = 4. (3 marks)
dy/dx = 2x − 3, so the gradient at x = 4 is 5 [1]; y(4) = 16 − 12 + 2 = 6, so the point is (4, 6) [1]; y − 6 = 5(x − 4), so y = 5x − 14 [1].
Find the coordinates of the points on y = x³ − 12x where the tangent is horizontal. (3 marks)
dy/dx = 3x² − 12 [1]; 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 2 or x = −2 [1]; the points are (2, −16) and (−2, 16) [1].
Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x) = 3x² − x. (4 marks)
f(x + h) = 3(x² + 2xh + h²) − x − h [1]; f(x + h) − f(x) = 6xh + 3h² − h [1]; dividing by h gives 6x + 3h − 1 [1]; as h → 0, f′(x) = 6x − 1 [1].
Let f(x) = x³ − 2x. Find the average rate of change of f from x = 1 to x = 3, and the instantaneous rate of change at x = 2. (2 marks)
The curve y = x² + bx + c has a stationary point at (2, −1). Find b and c. (3 marks)
dy/dx = 2x + b [1]; stationary at x = 2: 4 + b = 0, so b = −4 [1]; y(2) = 4 − 8 + c = −1, so c = 3 [1].
Find the points on the curve y = x³ − 3x² + 2 at which the tangent is parallel to the line y = 9x + 5. (4 marks)
The required gradient is 9 [1]; dy/dx = 3x² − 6x [1]; 3x² − 6x = 9 gives (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1 [1]; the points are (3, 2) and (−1, −2) [1].
A particle moves so that its position is s(t) = t³ − 9t² + 24t metres at t seconds. Find its velocity function, the times when it is momentarily at rest, and its positions at those times. (3 marks)
Find the values of x for which f(x) = x² − 6x is decreasing. (2 marks)
f′(x) = 2x − 6 [1]; f is decreasing when f′(x) < 0, that is x < 3 [1].
The curve y = ax³ + bx passes through (1, 5) and has gradient 7 at x = 1. Find a and b. (3 marks)
From the point: a + b = 5 [1]; dy/dx = 3ax² + b, so 3a + b = 7 [1]; subtracting gives 2a = 2, so a = 1 and b = 4 [1].
If f(x) = 5x⁴ − 2x³ + x, then f′(1) equals
f′(x) = 20x³ − 6x² + 1, so f′(1) = 20 − 6 + 1 = 15. Option 14 drops the derivative of x, which is 1.
f′(x) = 6x − 6, so f′(−1) = −6 − 6 = −12. Substituting x = −1 into f(x) instead of f′(x) would give 10, which is the value of the function, not the gradient.
The derivative of f(x) = x(x² − 4) is
Expand first: f(x) = x³ − 4x, so f′(x) = 3x² − 4. Differentiating only the bracket gives 2x, which is wrong because x is also a factor.
The gradient of y = 2x³ − x² equals 8 when
dy/dx = 6x² − 2x = 8 gives 3x² − x − 4 = 0, so (3x − 4)(x + 1) = 0 and x = 4/3 or x = −1. Both solutions are valid, so stating only one is incomplete.
For x ≠ 3, let f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3). Then f′(x) equals
Since x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), f(x) = x + 3 for x ≠ 3, so f′(x) = 1. Option x + 3 is the simplified function, not its derivative.
The function f(x) = 4x − x³ is increasing when
f′(x) = 4 − 3x² > 0 gives x² < 4/3, so −2/√3 < x < 2/√3. The outer intervals are where f′(x) < 0, so the function is decreasing there.
Using first principles, for f(x) = x² the expression (f(x + h) − f(x))/h simplifies to
(x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h², and dividing by h gives 2x + h. The limit as h → 0 is 2x, but the expression itself still contains h.
The function f(x) = 3x² + kx has f′(2) = 14. The value of k is
f′(x) = 6x + k, so f′(2) = 12 + k = 14 and k = 2. Option 12 is the value of 6x at x = 2, not k.
The position of a cyclist is s(t) = t³ − 3t metres at time t seconds. Her velocity when t = 2 is
v(t) = s′(t) = 3t² − 3, so v(2) = 12 − 3 = 9 m s⁻¹. Option 2 m s⁻¹ is the position s(2) = 8 − 6 = 2 m, not the velocity.
The derivative of f(x) = x²(3 − x) is
Expand: f(x) = 3x² − x³, so f′(x) = 6x − 3x². Differentiating each factor separately and multiplying is not valid.
The derivative of f(x) = ½x⁴ − 2x² is
Multiply by the power and reduce it by one: ½ × 4x³ = 2x³ and 2 × 2x = 4x, giving 2x³ − 4x. Forgetting the coefficient ½ gives 4x³ − 4x.
On the curve y = x² − 6x + 5, the gradient is −2 at the point
dy/dx = 2x − 6 = −2 gives x = 2, and y = 4 − 12 + 5 = −3. The point (2, −2) has the correct x-value but a wrongly calculated y-value.
Let f(x) = x⁴ − 4x². Find f′(x) and hence the values of x for which f′(x) = 0. (3 marks)
The curve y = ax² − 3x has gradient 9 at x = 2. Find the value of a. (2 marks)
Let f(x) = (x² − 3x)(x + 2). Expand f(x), then find f′(x) and the value of f′(1). (3 marks)
The volume of water in a tank is V(t) = 100 + 12t − t² litres, t minutes after a tap is opened. Find V′(t) and the time at which the volume stops increasing. (3 marks)
V′(t) = 12 − 2t [1]; the volume stops increasing when V′(t) = 0 [1]; 12 − 2t = 0, so t = 6 minutes [1].
Find the values of x for which f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x is increasing. (3 marks)
f′(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1) [1]; f is increasing when f′(x) > 0 [1]; so x < −1 or x > 3 [1].
Find the gradient of the curve y = x²(x − 3) at each of its x-intercepts. (3 marks)
y = x³ − 3x², so x-intercepts are x = 0 and x = 3 [1]; dy/dx = 3x² − 6x [1]; gradient is 0 at x = 0 and 27 − 18 = 9 at x = 3 [1].
For f(x) = x² − 4x, find the value of c between x = 1 and x = 4 at which the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over [1, 4]. (3 marks)
Expand first: f(x) = 2x³ − x² + 6x − 3, so f′(x) = 6x² − 2x + 6. Multiplying the derivatives of the factors (2 × 2x) is wrong.

The equation of the tangent to y = x² − 3x at x = 2 is
y = x − 4
y = x − 2
y = x + 4
At x = 2, y = 4 − 6 = −2 and dy/dx = 2x − 3 = 1. Tangent: y + 2 = 1(x − 2), so y = x − 4.
methods12a3-ts-2
The function f(x) = x³ − 12x has a local minimum at
f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = ±2. f(2) = 8 − 24 = −16 and f(−2) = 16. The gradient changes from negative to positive at x = 2, so (2, −16) is the local minimum and (−2, 16) is the local maximum.
methods12a3-ts-3
At x = a the gradient of a curve changes from negative to positive. The point (a, f(a)) is
a local maximum
a stationary point of inflection
a local minimum
a point of discontinuity
A change from negative to positive gradient indicates a local minimum. A stationary point of inflection has the same sign of gradient on both sides.
methods12a3-ts-4
What is the gradient of the normal to y = x² at the point where x = 1?
The tangent gradient is 2x = 2. The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal, −1/2.
methods12a3-ts-5
The curve y = x² − 6x + k has its stationary point on the x-axis. The value of k is
dy/dx = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3. For y = 0 at x = 3: 9 − 18 + k = 0, so k = 9. (The curve is y = (x − 3)².)
methods12a3-ts-6
Find the equations of the tangent and the normal to y = x³ − 2x + 1 at the point where x = 2. (4 marks)
y(2) = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5 (1 mark); dy/dx = 3x² − 2 = 10 at x = 2 (1 mark); tangent: y − 5 = 10(x − 2), so y = 10x − 15 (1 mark); normal gradient −1/10: y − 5 = −(1/10)(x − 2), so x + 10y = 52 (1 mark).
methods12a3-ts-7
For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x, find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature. (4 marks)

f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3) = 0 gives x = 1 or x = 3 (1 mark); f(1) = 4 and f(3) = 0, so points (1, 4) and (3, 0) (1 mark); sign of f′: positive for x < 1, negative for 1 < x < 3, positive for x > 3 (1 mark); so (1, 4) is a local maximum and (3, 0) is a local minimum (1 mark).
methods12a3-ts-8
The tangent to y = x² + ax at the point where x = 1 is parallel to the line y = 4x + 3. Find a and the equation of the tangent. (3 marks)
dy/dx = 2x + a; at x = 1 this equals the line's gradient 4, so 2 + a = 4 and a = 2 (1 mark); y(1) = 1 + 2 = 3, so the point is (1, 3) (1 mark); tangent: y − 3 = 4(x − 1), so y = 4x − 1 (1 mark).
methods12a3-ts-9
The gradient of the tangent to y = x³ at the point where x = −2 is
dy/dx = 3x², so at x = −2 the gradient is 3(4) = 12. A negative answer comes from forgetting that (−2)² is positive.
methods12a3-ts-10
The x-coordinate of the stationary point of f(x) = x² − 4x + 7 is
f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2. The value 4 is the coefficient of x, not the solution of f′(x) = 0.
methods12a3-ts-11
The equation of the tangent to y = x² + 1 at x = 1 is
y = x + 1
y = 2x
y(1) = 2 and dy/dx = 2x = 2 at x = 1. Tangent: y − 2 = 2(x − 1), so y = 2x.
methods12a3-ts-12
The equation of the normal to y = x² − 4x at the point where x = 3 is
y(3) = −3 and dy/dx = 2x − 4 = 2, so the normal gradient is −½. Normal: y + 3 = −½(x − 3), so y = −½x − 3/2. The line y = 2x − 9 is the tangent.
methods12a3-ts-13
The number of stationary points of y = x³ + 3x is
dy/dx = 3x² + 3 = 3(x² + 1) is always positive, so it is never zero and there are no stationary points. Setting 3x² + 3 = 0 does not give x = ±1 because x² = −1 has no real solutions.
methods12a3-ts-14
The maximum value of f(x) = −x² + 6x is
f′(x) = −2x + 6 = 0 gives x = 3, and f(3) = −9 + 18 = 9. The value 3 is where the maximum occurs, not the maximum value.
methods12a3-ts-15
The tangent to y = x² − 2x is parallel to the line y = 6x − 1 at the point where x equals
dy/dx = 2x − 2 must equal 6, so 2x = 8 and x = 4. Using x = 3 would come from solving 2x = 6 and forgetting the −2.
methods12a3-ts-16
The tangent to y = x² is perpendicular to the line y = −x/3 + 2 at the point where x equals
The line has gradient −1/3, so the tangent gradient is 3. Then 2x = 3 gives x = 3/2. Using x = 3 forgets that dy/dx = 2x.
methods12a3-ts-17
The tangent to y = x² at x = 3 crosses the x-axis at x =
y(3) = 9 and the gradient is 6, so the tangent is y = 6x − 9. Setting y = 0 gives x = 3/2. The curve touches the axis only at x = 0, not at the tangent's intercept.
methods12a3-ts-18
The x-values of the stationary points of f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x are
x = −1 and x = −2
x = 1 and x = −2
x = 1 and x = 2
x = 2 only
f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 1 or x = 2. The signs are wrong in the options with negative values.
methods12a3-ts-19

methods12a3-ts-20
A function has f′(2) = 0 and f′(x) > 0 on both sides of x = 2. The point where x = 2 is
a stationary point of inflection

Explain how differentiation can be used to check that F(x) = x⁴/2 − 3x² + 7x is an antiderivative of f(x) = 2x³ − 6x + 7. (2 marks)
Differentiate F: F′(x) = 2x³ − 6x + 7 [1]; since F′(x) = f(x), F is an antiderivative of f [1].
Add 1 to each power and divide by the new power: 2x⁴/4 − 3x²/2 + c = x⁴/2 − 3x²/2 + c. Dividing the second term by 2 is needed, so 3x² alone is wrong.

Given that f′(x) = 9x² − 4x + 1 and f(−1) = 2, find f(x). (3 marks)
The rate of change of the volume of water in a tank is dV/dt = 6t − 0.3t² litres per minute, and V(0) = 50 litres. Find V(t) and the volume at t = 10. (3 marks)
Given f′(x) = 3x² − 4x + 1 and f(1) = 5, find f(x).
Antidifferentiate: f(x) = x³ − 2x² + x + c. f(1) = 1 − 2 + 1 + c = c = 5.
vce-methods12-challenge: For which values of k does kx² + 4x + k = 0 have two distinct real solutions?
Δ = 16 − 4k² > 0 gives k² < 4. k = 0 makes the equation linear (one solution), so it is excluded.
Let u = 2^x: u² − 5u + 4 = 0, so u = 1 or 4. 2^x = 1 gives x = 0; 2^x = 4 gives x = 2.
If f(x) = x³ + 1, then f⁻¹(9) equals:

Both (x − 1) and (x + 1) are factors. P(1) = 1 + a + b − 2 = 0 and P(−1) = −1 + a − b − 2 = 0 give a + b = 1 and a − b = 3. Check: x³ + 2x² − x − 2 = (x + 2)(x² − 1).

X.title: A parabola, a line and a tangent
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Express \(f(x)\) in turning point form, and state the coordinates of the turning point.

steps.working: In the form \(a(x - h)^2 + k\) the turning point is \((h, k) = (2, -1)\).

pieces.mistake: Reading the turning point as \((-2, -1)\). In \((x - h)^2\) the \(x\)-coordinate is \(+h\), so \((x - 2)^2\) gives \(x = 2\).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the \(x\)-intercepts of the graph of \(y = f(x)\).
pieces.mistake: Getting the signs wrong when factorising: the factors must multiply to \(+3\) and add to \(-4\), so they are \(-1\) and \(-3\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of \(y = f(x)\) at the point where \(x = 4\).
pieces.mistake: Using \(f(4)\) as the gradient. The gradient of the tangent is \(f'(4)\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the coordinates of the points where the line \(y = x - 1\) meets the graph of \(y = f(x)\).

steps.working: Substitute into \(y = x - 1\): the points are \((1, 0)\) and \((4, 3)\).

pieces.mistake: Giving only the \(x\)-values. The question asks for coordinates, so find \(y\) as well.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is translated 2 units to the left and 1 unit up. Find the rule of the image.

steps.working: A translation 2 units left replaces \(x\) with \(x + 2\), and 1 unit up adds 1: \(y = f(x + 2) + 1\).

pieces.mistake: Replacing \(x\) with \(x - 2\) for a move to the left. Moving left by 2 means replacing \(x\) with \(x + 2\).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find the average rate of change of \(f\) between \(x = 0\) and \(x = 4\).
pieces.mistake: Finding the instantaneous rate of change at one point, such as \(f'(4)\). The average rate of change uses the two end points.

X.title: Growing bacteria and contaminated dishes
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: The number of bacteria in a culture \(t\) hours after an experiment starts is \(N(t) = 500 \times 2^{t/3}\).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the number of bacteria at the start of the experiment.
pieces.mistake: Taking \(2^0\) to be 0. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the number of bacteria after 6 hours.
pieces.mistake: Multiplying 500 by \(\frac{6}{3} = 2\) instead of using it as a power. \(2^{6/3} = 2^2 = 4\), so the number has doubled twice.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find how long it takes for the number of bacteria to reach 8000.
pieces.mistake: Dividing 8000 by 500 and then by 2, as if the growth were linear. The number doubles every 3 hours, so write 16 as a power of 2.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: The rule can also be written as \(N(t) = 500e^{kt}\). Find the exact value of \(k\).

steps.working: Write the base 2 as a power of \(e\): \(2 = e^{\log_e 2}\), so \(2^{t/3} = e^{\frac{t}{3}\log_e 2}\).

pieces.mistake: Writing \(k = \log_e \frac{2}{3}\). The 3 divides the whole logarithm: \(k = \frac{1}{3}\log_e 2\).

pieces.text: A laboratory has 10 culture dishes. Seven are growing normally and three are contaminated. Two dishes are chosen at random, without replacement.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the probability that both dishes are contaminated.

steps.working: \(\Pr(\text{first contaminated}) = \frac{3}{10}\); then 2 of the remaining 9 are contaminated, so the second has probability \(\frac{2}{9}\).

pieces.mistake: Using \(\frac{3}{10} \times \frac{3}{10}\). Without replacement, the second probability changes to \(\frac{2}{9}\).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find the probability that exactly one of the dishes is contaminated.

steps.working: Exactly one can happen two ways: contaminated then normal, \(\frac{3}{10} \times \frac{7}{9}\), or normal then contaminated, \(\frac{7}{10} \times \frac{3}{9}\).

pieces.mistake: Counting only one order. 'Exactly one' includes both orders, so add the two branches.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: Given that at least one of the dishes is contaminated, find the probability that both are contaminated.
pieces.mistake: Dividing by the probability of exactly one (\(\frac{7}{15}\)). The given event is 'at least one', which also includes 'both'.

X.title: A Ferris wheel
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: The height, \(h\) metres, of a seat on a Ferris wheel \(t\) minutes after the ride starts is \(h(t) = 20 - 18\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)\), \(t \ge 0\).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the minimum height, the maximum height and the period of the rotation.
pieces.answer: Minimum 2 m, maximum 38 m, period 30 minutes
pieces.mistake: Giving the period as \(\frac{\pi}{15}\). Period = \(2\pi\) divided by the coefficient of \(t\).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the height of the seat after 5 minutes.
pieces.mistake: Using \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). That is \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the first time at which the seat is 29 m above the ground.

steps.working: The first solution is \(\frac{\pi t}{15} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), so \(t = 10\) minutes.

pieces.mistake: Taking \(\frac{\pi t}{15} = \frac{\pi}{3}\), which solves \(\cos = +\frac{1}{2}\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the average rate of change of height over the first 5 minutes.
pieces.mistake: Dividing 11 by 5. The seat starts at 2 m, not 0 m.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: During one rotation, for how long is the seat more than 29 m above the ground?

steps.working: So \(10 < t < 20\): the seat is above 29 m for 10 minutes of each rotation.

pieces.mistake: Finding only the first time (10 minutes). The question asks for a duration, so find when it drops below 29 m again.

X.title: A cubic and a bag of balls
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Use the factor theorem to show that \(x - 3\) is a factor of \(p(x)\).

steps.working: \(p(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 27 = 0\); by the factor theorem, \(x - 3\) is a factor.

pieces.mistake: Substituting \(x = -3\). For the factor \(x - 3\), substitute \(x = 3\).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Factorise \(p(x)\) fully and state the solutions of \(p(x) = 0\).
pieces.mistake: Stopping at \((x - 3)(x^2 - 9)\). \(x^2 - 9\) is a difference of two squares.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of \(y = p(x)\) and state their nature.
pieces.answer: \((-1, 32)\), a local maximum; \((3, 0)\), a local minimum

steps.working: For a positive cubic, the first stationary point is a local maximum and the second a local minimum: \((-1, 32)\) maximum, \((3, 0)\) minimum.

pieces.mistake: Forgetting to substitute back into \(p(x)\) for the \(y\)-coordinates.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find an antiderivative of \(p(x)\).

steps.working: Increase each power by 1 and divide by the new power: \(\frac{x^4}{4} - x^3 - \frac{9x^2}{2} + 27x + c\).

pieces.mistake: Differentiating instead of antidifferentiating.

pieces.text: A bag contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are taken out at random without replacement.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the probability that both balls are the same colour.
pieces.mistake: Using \(\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{3}{5}\). Without replacement, the second probability changes.

pieces.question: Show that (x − 3) is a factor of f(x), and hence factorise f(x) fully.
pieces.mistake: Stopping at (x − 3)(x² − 9) without factorising further.

pieces.label: c

pieces.label: d

pieces.mistake: Using f(1) as the gradient.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: For which values of k does f(x) = k have exactly three solutions?

steps.working: A horizontal line meets the graph three times strictly between the local minimum and local maximum values.

pieces.mistake: Including k = 0 or k = 32, which give only two solutions.

pieces.text: The height of a cabin on a Ferris wheel, h metres, t minutes after a ride starts is h(t) = 22 − 20cos(πt/10), for t ≥ 0.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the maximum and minimum heights of the cabin.

steps.working: cos ranges from −1 to 1, so h ranges over 22 ± 20.

pieces.mistake: Giving 20 m as the maximum (the amplitude).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: How long does one full revolution take?
pieces.mistake: Answering 10 minutes.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find when the cabin first reaches a height of 32 m.

steps.working: The first solution is πt/10 = 2π/3, so t = 20/3 ≈ 6.67 min.

pieces.mistake: Taking πt/10 = π/3, where cosine is positive.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: For how long in each revolution is the cabin above 32 m?

steps.working: So 20/3 < t < 40/3, a duration of 20/3 ≈ 6.67 minutes.

pieces.mistake: Finding only the first time and not the interval.

pieces.text: The wheel has 12 cabins, 3 of which are VIP cabins. Four friends are each randomly assigned a different cabin.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the probability that at least one friend gets a VIP cabin, correct to three decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Calculating 4 × 3/12 = 1, which double-counts.
